title: VI. The Prosecutor’s Speech. Sketches Of Character
paragraphs: Ippolit Kirillovitch began his speech trembling with nerves, cold sweat on his forehead, flashing hot and cold by turns. He said so himself afterward. He considered this speech his masterpiece — the masterpiece of his whole life, his swan song. And in fact he died nine months later of galloping consumption, so it turned out he'd had the right to compare himself to a swan singing its last song. He had put his whole heart and every ounce of brain he had into that speech. And to everyone's surprise, poor Ippolit Kirillovitch turned out to have at least some genuine feeling for the public good and for “the eternal question” hidden away in him. What really set his speech apart was its sincerity. He truly believed the prisoner was guilty; he wasn't prosecuting merely as an official duty, and when he called for retribution he trembled with real passion “for the safety of society.” Even the women in the audience, who stayed hostile to Ippolit Kirillovitch throughout, admitted he made an extraordinary impression on them. He began in a cracking voice, but it gained strength as he went and filled the courtroom by the end of his speech. Yet the moment he finished, he nearly fainted.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” the prosecutor began, “this case has caused a stir across all of Russia. But what is there to be amazed at, really — what is so uniquely horrifying about it to us? That's what's so horrifying: that we've grown so used to crimes like this. What ought to appall us is not this or that isolated crime, but the fact that we've become accustomed to it. What accounts for our indifference, our lukewarm response to acts like this, to these signs of the times, ominous as they are for an unpromising future? Is it cynicism? Is it a premature exhaustion of intellect and imagination in a society sinking into decay despite its youth? Is it that our moral principles have been shaken to their foundations, or perhaps that we have no such principles at all? I can't answer these questions, and yet they trouble me, and every citizen not only must but ought to be troubled by them. Our young and still timid press has already done the public a real service, because without it we would never have learned of the horrors of unchecked violence and moral collapse that the papers keep bringing to light — not just to those who attend the new jury courts set up under the present reign, but to everyone. And what do we read almost every day? Things next to which this case pales, seems almost ordinary. But the important point is that most of our national crimes of violence testify to a widespread evil, now so general among us that it's hard to fight.”

“One day we see a brilliant young officer from high society, at the very start of his career, coldly and treacherously, without a flicker of conscience, murdering an official who had once been his benefactor, along with the man's servant girl, in order to steal his own promissory note and whatever cash he could find on him — ‘it'll come in handy for my pleasures in fashionable society, and for my career.’ After killing them, he tucks a pillow under each victim's head, then leaves. Next, a young war hero ‘decorated for bravery’ kills the mother of his commanding officer and benefactor, like a common highwayman, and to talk his accomplices into it he insists that ‘she loves him like a son, so she'll follow all his instructions and take no precautions.’ Granted, he's a monster — but I don't dare claim these days that he's unique. Another man won't commit the murder, but will feel and think exactly as he does, and is every bit as rotten in his soul. Alone, in silence, with only his conscience for company, he may ask himself, ‘What is honor, really — and isn't condemning bloodshed just a prejudice?’”

“Perhaps people will accuse me of being morbid, hysterical, of monstrous slander, of exaggeration. Let them say so — and heaven knows, I'd be the first to rejoice if it were true! Oh, don't believe me — think of me as sick in the head if you like, but remember my words: even if only a tenth, only a twentieth, of what I say is true, it's still appalling! Look how our young people kill themselves, without so much as asking Hamlet's question about what lies beyond, without any sign that such a question has crossed their minds — as though everything to do with the soul, with what awaits us past the grave, had long ago been erased from their heads and buried in the sand. Look at our vice, our libertines. Fyodor Pavlovitch, the unlucky victim in this case, was practically an innocent babe next to many of them. And yet we all knew him — ‘he lived among us!’...”

“Yes — perhaps someday the great minds of Russia and of Europe will study the psychology of Russian crime, because the subject deserves it. But that study will come later, at leisure, once all of today's tragic upheaval lies further behind us, when it can be examined with more insight and more fairness than I can manage now. For the moment we're either horrified, or pretend to be, while actually gloating over the spectacle, drawn to strong and eccentric sensations that titillate our cynical, pampered boredom. Or else, like children, we brush the terrible ghosts away and bury our heads in the pillow, eager to get back to our games and amusements the moment they're gone. But someday we'll have to start living in sober earnest; we'll have to look at ourselves as a society; it's time we tried to understand something of our own social condition, or at least made a start in that direction.”

“A great writer of the last generation, comparing Russia to a swift troika racing toward an unknown destination, cries out, ‘Oh, troika, bird-like troika, who invented you!’ and adds, in proud ecstasy, that all the nations of the world stand respectfully aside to let the recklessly galloping troika pass. Maybe so — maybe they do stand aside, respectfully or not — but in my humble opinion the great writer ended his book that way either in a fit of childish, naïve optimism, or simply out of fear of the censors of his day. Because if the troika were being driven by his own heroes — Sobakevitch, Nozdryov, Tchitchikov — it could never reach any rational destination, no matter who held the reins. And those were the heroes of an older generation. Ours are worse specimens still....”

At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch's speech was interrupted by applause. The liberal implications of the image were not lost on anyone. The applause was brief, true, so the presiding judge didn't think it necessary to issue a warning, and only gave the offenders a stern look. But Ippolit Kirillovitch was encouraged — he had never been applauded before! All his life he had struggled to get anyone to listen to him, and now, suddenly, he had a chance to command the ear of all Russia.

“What, in the end, is this Karamazov family, which has earned such an unenviable notoriety across Russia?” he went on. “Perhaps I'm exaggerating, but it seems to me that certain fundamental traits of today's educated class are reflected in this family portrait — only, of course, in miniature, ‘like the sun in a drop of water.’ Think of that unhappy, depraved, unrestrained old man who met such a grim end — the head of a family! Born into the nobility, but in a poor, dependent position, he came into a small fortune through an unexpected marriage. A petty schemer, a toady and a buffoon, with a fairly sharp though undeveloped mind, he was above all a moneylender, growing bolder as his fortunes grew. His fawning, servile side dropped away, leaving only his malicious, sarcastic cynicism. Spiritually he never developed at all, while his appetite for life was excessive. He saw nothing in life but sensual pleasure, and he raised his children to see nothing else either. He felt no obligation to his duties as a father — he mocked them. He left his young children to the servants and was glad to be rid of them, forgot about them entirely. The old man's motto was Après moi le déluge. He stood for everything opposed to civic duty, the most complete and vicious individualism. ‘Let the world burn, so long as I'm all right’ — and he was all right; he was content, eager to keep living exactly this way for another twenty or thirty years. He cheated his own son, spending the boy's money — his inheritance from his mother — trying to steal his mistress from him. No, I don't intend to leave the prisoner's defense entirely to my talented colleague from Petersburg. I'll speak the truth myself: I understand perfectly well what resentment must have built up in the son's heart against him.”

“But enough, enough about that unhappy old man — he's paid the price. Let's remember, though, that he was a father, and one of the typical fathers of our time. Am I really being unfair in calling him typical of a great many modern fathers? Alas — plenty of them differ from him only in not openly flaunting such cynicism, because they're better educated, more cultured, but their underlying philosophy is essentially the same as his. Perhaps I'm a pessimist — but you've agreed to forgive me that. Let's agree in advance: you don't have to believe me, but let me speak. Let me say what I have to say, and hold on to a little of it.”
“Now, the children of this father, this head of a family. One of them is the prisoner before us — the rest of my speech will deal with him. Of the other two I'll speak only in passing.”

“The eldest son is one of those modern young men of brilliant education and vigorous intellect who has lost all faith in everything. He has already denied and rejected a great deal, like his father. We've all heard him speak; he was a welcome guest in local society. He never hid his views — quite the opposite, in fact — which is my justification for speaking rather openly about him now, not as an individual, of course, but as a member of the Karamazov family. Another figure closely tied to this case took his own life here just last night. I mean the afflicted, feeble-minded man who had been Fyodor Pavlovitch's servant, and possibly his illegitimate son — Smerdyakov. At the preliminary inquiry he told me, in tears, hysterically, how young Ivan Karamazov had appalled him with his spiritual daring. ‘Everything in the world is permitted, according to him, and nothing will be forbidden from now on — that's what he always taught me.’ I believe that poor, feeble-minded man was driven out of his senses by this theory, though of course the epileptic fits he suffered from, and this terrible catastrophe, no doubt helped unhinge his mind further. But he let drop one remark, quite striking, that would have done credit to a more intelligent observer, and that's exactly why I mention it: ‘If there's one of the sons who takes after Fyodor Pavlovitch in character, it's Ivan Fyodorovitch.’”

“With that remark I'll close my sketch of his character — I feel it would be indelicate to go further. Oh, I have no wish to draw further conclusions and croak over the young man's future like some raven of doom. We've seen today, in this courtroom, that there are still good impulses in his young heart, that family feeling has not been destroyed in him by his lack of faith and his cynicism — traits that came to him more by inheritance, I think, than through any exercise of his own independent thought.”

“Then the third son. Oh, he's a devout, modest young man, who doesn't share his elder brother's bleak, destructive view of life. He has tried to hold fast to ‘the ideas of the people,’ or to whatever goes by that name in certain circles of our educated class. He clung to the monastery, and came within a hair of becoming a monk. It seems to me he unconsciously betrayed, and at such an early age, that timid despair which drives so many in our unhappy society — people who dread cynicism and its corrupting influence, and mistakenly blame all our troubles on European enlightenment — to return to their ‘native soil,’ as they call it, to the bosom, so to speak, of their mother earth, like frightened children longing to fall asleep against the withered breast of their aged mother, and to sleep there forever, if only to escape the horrors that terrify them.”

“For my part, I wish the excellent, gifted young man every success. I hope his youthful idealism and his pull toward the ideas of the people never degenerate, as so often happens, into gloomy mysticism on the spiritual side and blind chauvinism on the political — two forces that pose an even greater danger to Russia than the premature decay, born of misunderstanding and the wholesale borrowing of European ideas, from which his elder brother is suffering.”

Two or three people clapped at the mention of chauvinism and mysticism. Ippolit Kirillovitch had, in truth, been swept away by his own eloquence. None of this had much to do with the case at hand — not to mention that it was rather vague — but the sickly, consumptive man was overcome by the urge to express himself, just once, in his life. People said afterward that his criticism of Ivan was driven by less than noble motives, since Ivan had gotten the better of him once or twice in argument, and Ippolit Kirillovitch, remembering it, was now taking his revenge. But I don't know whether that's true. In any case, all this was only introductory, and the speech now moved on to a more direct look at the case.

“But to return to the eldest son,” Ippolit Kirillovitch went on. “He is the prisoner before us. We have his life, and his actions too, laid out before us; the fatal day has come, and everything has risen to the surface. While his brothers seem to stand for ‘Europeanism’ and ‘the principles of the people,’ he seems to represent Russia as she actually is. Oh, not all of Russia — not all of her! God forbid it should be so! And yet here she is, our mother Russia, her very scent and sound. Oh, he is spontaneous — a marvelous jumble of good and evil, a lover of culture and of Schiller, and yet he brawls in taverns and yanks the beards of his drinking companions. Oh, he too can be good, even noble — but only when things are going well for him. What's more, he can be swept off his feet, positively carried away, by noble ideals — but only if they come to him unbidden, if they drop from heaven, if he doesn't have to pay for them. He hates paying for anything, but he loves receiving, and that's true of him in everything. Oh, give him every good thing life has to offer — he wouldn't be satisfied with less — put no obstacle in his way, and he'll show you that he too can be noble. He isn't greedy — no — but he has to have money, a great deal of money, and you'll see how generously, with what contempt for filthy lucre, he'll fling it all away in one night of reckless dissipation. But if he has no money, you'll see what he's prepared to do to get it when he needs it badly enough. But all that comes later — let's take events in their order.”

“First we have before us a poor, neglected child, running around the back yard ‘without boots on his feet,’ as our worthy and esteemed fellow citizen of foreign extraction — alas! — put it just now. I say again, I yield the defense of the accused to no one. I am here to accuse him, but to defend him too. Yes, I too am human; I too can weigh the influence of home and childhood on a man's character. But the boy grows up and becomes an officer; for a duel, and other reckless behavior, he's exiled to one of Russia's remote frontier towns. There he led the wild life of an officer. And of course he needed money — money above everything — and so, after long disputes, he came to a settlement with his father, and the last six thousand roubles were sent to him. There's a letter in existence in which he essentially waives his claim to the rest and settles his dispute with his father over the inheritance for that payment of six thousand.”

“Then came his meeting with a young woman of lofty character and brilliant education. Oh, I won't presume to repeat the details — you've only just heard them. Honor, self-sacrifice, were on display there, and I'll say no more. The figure of the young officer, frivolous and dissolute, paying homage to true nobility and a lofty ideal, appeared before us in a very sympathetic light. But the other side of the coin was unexpectedly turned toward us immediately afterward, in this very courtroom. Again I won't venture to guess why it happened that way, but there were reasons. That same lady, her eyes wet with tears of long-suppressed indignation, told us that he — he, of all men — had despised her for an act which, reckless and imprudent as it may have been, was still prompted by lofty and generous motives. He, the girl's own betrothed, looked at her with that mocking smile, more unbearable coming from him than from anyone else. And knowing already that he had deceived her — believing, as he did, that she was bound to endure anything from him, even betrayal — she deliberately offered him three thousand roubles, and let him understand, all too clearly, that she was paying him to deceive her. ‘Well — will you take it or not? Have you no shame at all?’ was the silent question in her searching eyes. He looked at her, saw plainly what was in her mind — he's admitted before you here that he understood all of it — and pocketed those three thousand roubles without a second thought, then squandered them in two days on his new love.”

“What are we to believe, then? The first version — of the young officer sacrificing his last farthing in a noble burst of generosity, doing homage to virtue — or this other, repellent picture? As a rule, when faced with two extremes, one looks for the middle ground — but in this case that won't do. It's more likely that in the first instance he was genuinely noble, and in the second, genuinely base. And why? Because he has the broad Karamazov nature — that's exactly what I'm building toward — capable of combining the most incongruous contradictions, capable of the greatest heights and the greatest depths at once. Remember the brilliant observation made by a young man who has watched the Karamazov family up close — Mr. Rakitin: ‘The sense of their own degradation is as essential to these reckless, ungoverned natures as the sense of their own lofty generosity.’ And that's true — they need this unnatural mixture continually. Two extremes at the same moment, or else they feel wretched, dissatisfied, incomplete. They are as broad as mother Russia herself; they take in everything and endure everything.”

“By the way, gentlemen of the jury, since we've just touched on those three thousand roubles, I'll venture to get a little ahead of myself. Can you really imagine a man like that — having received that sum, and in such a way, at the cost of such shame, such disgrace, such utter degradation — could have been capable, that very same day, of setting aside half the sum, sewing it into a little bag, and having the strength of character to carry it on him for a whole month afterward, in spite of every temptation and his desperate need for it! Not once, whether in drunken debauchery in taverns, or when he was racing out into the countryside trying to borrow, from God knows whom, the money he so badly needed to keep the woman he loved out of his father's clutches, did he bring himself to touch that little bag! Why, if only to keep from abandoning his mistress to the rival he was so jealous of, he'd surely have opened that bag and stayed behind to watch over her, waiting for the moment she would finally say to him, ‘I am yours,’ so that he could fly off with her, far from those fatal surroundings.”

“But no — he never touched his talisman, and what reason does he give for that? The main reason, as I've just said, was that when she said ‘I am yours, take me wherever you like,’ he wanted to have the means to take her. But that first reason, in the prisoner's own words, mattered little next to the second. As long as I have that money on me, he said, I am a scoundrel, but not a thief — because I can always go to my insulted betrothed and, laying down half the sum I fraudulently took, say to her, ‘You see, I've squandered half your money, and shown myself weak and dishonorable, a scoundrel if you like’ (I'm using the prisoner's own words) ‘— but though I'm a scoundrel, I'm not a thief, because if I were a thief, I wouldn't have brought you back this half — I'd have taken it too, the way I took the rest!’ A remarkable explanation! This frantic but weak man, who couldn't resist the temptation of taking three thousand roubles at the price of such disgrace, suddenly develops the most stoical willpower and carries around a thousand roubles without daring to touch it. Does that square at all with the character we've just examined? No — and I'll go so far as to tell you how the real Dmitri Karamazov would have behaved in such circumstances, if he had actually brought himself to set the money aside.”

“At the very first temptation — say, to treat the woman with whom he'd already squandered half the money — he would have unpicked the little bag and pulled out a hundred roubles or so. Because why, exactly, would he have kept back precisely half the money — fifteen hundred roubles? Why not fourteen hundred? He could just as easily have claimed he wasn't a thief by bringing back fourteen hundred. Then, another time, he'd have unpicked it again and taken out another hundred, and then a third time, and a fourth, and before the month was out he'd have taken the second-to-last note, reasoning that bringing back even a hundred would serve the purpose, since a thief would have stolen the whole lot. And then he'd have looked at that last note and told himself, ‘It's really not worth handing back just a hundred — let's spend that too!’ That's how the real Dmitri Karamazov, as we know him, would have behaved. Nothing could be harder to reconcile with the actual facts than this legend of the little bag. Nothing could be less conceivable. But we'll return to that later.”

After touching on what had come out at the trial concerning the financial dealings between father and son, and arguing again and again that it was utterly impossible, from the known facts, to say which of them was in the wrong, Ippolit Kirillovitch moved on to the medical experts' testimony regarding Mitya's fixed idea about the three thousand roubles owed him.

title: VII. An Historical Survey
paragraphs: “The medical experts have tried to convince us that the prisoner is out of his mind — in fact, a maniac. I maintain that he is in full possession of his senses, and that if he weren't, he would have behaved more cleverly. As for his being a maniac, I'll grant that much, but only on one point: his fixed idea about the three thousand roubles. Even so, I think one could find a far simpler explanation than any tendency toward insanity. For my part, I fully agree with the young doctor who maintained that the prisoner's mental faculties have always been normal, and that he has simply been irritable and exasperated. The object of the prisoner's continual, violent anger was never the sum of money itself — there was a special motive underneath it. That motive is jealousy!”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch described at length the prisoner's fatal passion for Grushenka. He began with the moment the prisoner went to the ‘young woman's’ lodgings ‘to beat her’ — ‘I'm using his own words,’ the prosecutor explained — ‘but instead of beating her, he stayed there, at her feet. That was where the passion began. At the same time, the prisoner's father had fallen for the same young woman — a strange and fatal coincidence, since both of them lost their hearts to her at once, though both had known her before. And she inspired in both of them the same violent, characteristically Karamazov passion. We have her own confession: “I was laughing at both of them.” Yes — the sudden urge to make a joke of them came over her, and she conquered them both at once. The old man, who worshipped money, immediately set aside three thousand roubles as payment for a single visit from her — but soon after, he'd have been happy to lay his whole fortune and his name at her feet, if only she'd become his lawful wife. We have solid evidence of this. As for the prisoner, the tragedy of his fate is plain — it's right in front of us. But such was the young woman's “game.” The enchantress gave the unhappy young man no hope until the very last moment, when he knelt before her with hands already stained with his father's and rival's blood. That was the position he was in when he was arrested. “Send me to Siberia with him — I brought him to this, I am the one most to blame,” the woman herself cried, in genuine remorse, at the moment of his arrest.’

“The talented young man I've already mentioned, Mr. Rakitin, summed up this heroine in a few striking words: ‘She was disillusioned early in life, betrayed and ruined by a fiancé who seduced and abandoned her. She was left in poverty, cursed by her respectable family, and taken under the wing of a wealthy old man, whom to this day she still considers her benefactor. There may well have been a great deal of good in her young heart, but it was embittered too soon. She grew shrewd and started saving money. She became sarcastic and resentful toward society.’ After that sketch of her character, it's easy enough to understand how she might have laughed at both of them purely out of mischief, out of spite.”

“After a month of hopeless love and moral collapse, during which he betrayed his betrothed and misappropriated money entrusted to his honor, the prisoner was driven nearly to frenzy, nearly to madness, by relentless jealousy — of whom? His own father! And the worst part was that the crazy old man was luring and enticing the object of his son's affection with the very same three thousand roubles that the son regarded as his own, part of his inheritance from his mother, of which his father was cheating him. Yes, I admit — that was hard to bear. It might well drive a man mad. It wasn't the money itself, but the fact that this money was being used, with such revolting cynicism, to destroy his happiness!”
Then the prosecutor went on to describe how the idea of murdering his father had taken hold in the prisoner's mind, and backed up his theory with facts.

“At first he only talked about it in taverns — he talked about it all that month. Ah, he likes always having company around him, and he likes telling his companions everything, even his most diabolical and dangerous ideas; he likes sharing every thought with others, and for some reason expects the people he confides in to meet him with perfect sympathy, to enter into all his troubles and worries, to take his side and never oppose him in anything. If they don't, he flies into a rage and smashes up everything in the tavern.” (Then followed the anecdote about Captain Snegiryov.) “Those who heard the prisoner began at last to suspect he might mean more than idle threats, and that such a frenzy might turn talk into action.”
Here the prosecutor described the family's meeting at the monastery, the conversations with Alyosha, and the ugly scene of violence when the prisoner burst into his father's house just after dinner.

“I can't say for certain,” the prosecutor went on, “that the prisoner had fully made up his mind to murder his father before that incident. And yet the idea had occurred to him more than once, and he had dwelt on it — we have facts, witnesses, and his own words to prove it. I confess, gentlemen of the jury,” he added, “that until today I was uncertain whether to credit the prisoner with conscious premeditation. I was firmly convinced he had pictured that fatal moment beforehand — but only pictured it, entertained it as a possibility. He hadn't definitely worked out when or how he might commit the crime.”

“But I was uncertain only until today — until that fatal document was placed before the court just now. You yourselves heard that young lady's exclamation: ‘It's the plan — the program for the murder!’ That's how she described that wretched, drunken letter from the unfortunate prisoner. And in fact, from that letter, we can see that the murder was premeditated in its entirety. It was written two days beforehand, and so we now know, as a fact, that forty-eight hours before carrying out his terrible design, the prisoner swore that if he couldn't get money by the next day, he would murder his father to take the envelope with the notes from under his pillow, as soon as Ivan had left. ‘As soon as Ivan has gone away’ — you hear that? So he had thought it all through, weighing every circumstance, and he carried it out exactly as he had written it. The proof of premeditation is conclusive; the crime must have been committed for the sake of the money — that's stated plainly, written down, and signed. The prisoner doesn't deny his own signature.”

“I'll be told he was drunk when he wrote it. But that doesn't lessen the letter's value — quite the opposite: drunk, he wrote down what he had planned sober. If he hadn't planned it sober, he wouldn't have written it drunk. I'll be asked: then why did he talk about it in taverns? A man planning such a crime keeps quiet and holds it to himself. Yes — but he talked about it before he'd formed any plan, when he had only the desire, only the impulse toward it. Afterward he talked about it less. On the evening he wrote that letter, at the ‘Metropolis’ tavern, he was unusually silent, though he'd been drinking. He didn't play billiards; he sat in a corner and spoke to no one. True, he did turn a shopkeeper out of his seat, but that was done almost without thinking — he could never walk into a tavern without causing some kind of scene. It's true that once he'd made his final decision, he must have felt uneasy at having talked so much about his plan beforehand, worried that it might lead to his arrest and prosecution afterward. But there was nothing to be done — he couldn't take his words back. Still, his luck had served him before, and it would serve him again. He believed in his star, you understand! I should add, too, that he did a great deal to avoid the fatal catastrophe. ‘Tomorrow I'll try to borrow money from everyone,’ as he puts it in his own peculiar language, ‘and if they won't give it to me, there will be bloodshed.’”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch went into a detailed account of all Mitya's efforts to borrow money. He described the visit to Samsonov, the trip to Lyagavy. “Harassed, mocked, hungry, having sold his watch to pay for the journey (though he tells us he had fifteen hundred roubles on him at the time — a likely story), tormented by jealousy at having left the object of his affections back in town, suspecting she'd go to Fyodor Pavlovitch while he was away, he finally returned to town, only to discover, to his joy, that she hadn't gone near his father. He even walked her home to her protector himself. (Strangely enough, he doesn't seem to have been jealous of Samsonov — which is psychologically interesting.) Then he hurries back to his hiding place in the back gardens, and there learns that Smerdyakov is having a fit, that the other servant is ill — the coast is clear, and he knows the ‘signals’ — what a temptation! And still he resists it; he goes off instead to a lady who has been living in town for some time and is highly respected among us, Madame Hohlakov. That lady, who had long watched his career with pity, gave him the most sensible advice: to give up his dissipated life, his unseemly love affair, the waste of his youth and energy in tavern debauchery, and to head off to Siberia to the gold mines — ‘that would be an outlet for your restless energy, your romantic nature, your thirst for adventure.’”

After describing the outcome of that conversation, and the moment the prisoner learned that Grushenka had not, after all, stayed at Samsonov's — the sudden frenzy of the unlucky man, worn down by jealousy and nervous exhaustion, at the thought that she had deceived him and was now with his father — Ippolit Kirillovitch closed by dwelling on the fatal role of chance. “Had the maid told him her mistress was at Mokroe with her former lover, nothing would have happened. But she lost her head; all she could do was swear and protest that she knew nothing, and if the prisoner didn't kill her on the spot, it was only because he ran off in pursuit of his faithless mistress.”

“But notice — frantic as he was, he took a brass pestle with him. Why that? Why not some other weapon? Because he'd been turning his plan over and preparing himself for it for a full month, he would have snatched up whatever looked like a weapon caught his eye. He'd realized for a month that any such object would serve, so he recognized instantly, without hesitation, that this one would do the job. So it wasn't unconscious at all, wasn't involuntary, that he grabbed that fatal pestle. And then we find him in his father's garden — the coast clear, no witnesses, darkness and jealousy all around him. The suspicion that she was there, with him, with his rival, in his arms, maybe laughing at him at that very moment — it took his breath away. And it wasn't mere suspicion; the deception was open, obvious. She had to be there, in that lit room, behind the screen — and the unhappy man would have us believe that he crept up to the window, peeked in respectfully, and discreetly withdrew, for fear something terrible and improper might happen. And he tries to persuade us of that — us, who understand his character, who know his state of mind at that moment, and know that he knew the very signals that would let him walk straight into the house.” At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch broke off to give an exhaustive discussion of the suspected connection between Smerdyakov and the murder. He went into it very thoroughly, and everyone could tell that although he claimed to dismiss the suspicion, he thought the subject mattered a great deal.

title: VIII. A Treatise On Smerdyakov
paragraphs: “To begin with, where did this suspicion come from?” (Ippolit Kirillovitch began.) “The first person to cry out that Smerdyakov had committed the murder was the prisoner himself, at the moment of his arrest — and yet from that moment to this he hasn't produced a single fact to back up the charge, not the faintest hint of one. The charge is supported by only three people: the prisoner's two brothers, and Madame Svyetlov. The elder of the two brothers voiced his suspicions only today, and while he was, without question, in the grip of brain fever. But we know that for the past two months he fully shared our conviction of his brother's guilt and made no attempt to argue against it. More on that later. The younger brother has admitted he hasn't the slightest fact to support his idea of Smerdyakov's guilt, and has been led to that conclusion purely by the prisoner's own words and the look on his face. Yes — that astonishing piece of testimony was offered twice today, by him. Madame Svyetlov was even more astonishing: ‘Whatever the prisoner tells you, you must believe — he's not a man who lies.’ That is the whole of the evidence against Smerdyakov produced by these three people, all of them deeply invested in the prisoner's fate. And yet the theory of Smerdyakov's guilt has been noised about, has been maintained, and is still being maintained. Is that credible? Is it even conceivable?”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch thought it necessary to describe Smerdyakov's character, “a man who cut short his own life in a fit of insanity.” He portrayed him as a man of weak intellect with a smattering of education, thrown off balance by philosophical ideas above his level and by certain modern notions of duty, which he picked up in practice from the reckless life of his master — who was perhaps also his father — Fyodor Pavlovitch; and, in theory, from various odd philosophical conversations with his master's elder son, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who readily indulged in this pastime, probably out of boredom, or perhaps to amuse himself at the valet's expense. “He spoke to me himself about his state of mind during his last few days at his father's house,” Ippolit Kirillovitch explained; “but others have testified to it too — the prisoner himself, his brother, and the servant Grigory — that is, everyone who knew him well.”

“What's more, Smerdyakov, whose health had been undermined by his epileptic attacks, had no more courage than a chicken. ‘He fell at my feet and kissed them,’ the prisoner himself has told us, before he realized how damaging that statement was to his own case. ‘He's an epileptic chicken,’ was how he characteristically described him. And the prisoner chose him as his confidant — we have his own word on it — and frightened him into finally agreeing to act as his spy. In that role he betrayed his master, revealing to the prisoner the existence of the envelope full of notes, and the signals that would let him into the house. How could he help telling him, really? ‘He would have killed me — I could see he would have killed me,’ Smerdyakov said at the inquiry, trembling and shaking even in front of us, though by then his tormentor had already been arrested and could do him no harm. ‘He suspected me every single moment. In fear and trembling I hurried to tell him every secret, just to calm him down, so he'd see I hadn't deceived him and would let me live.’ Those are his own words. I wrote them down, and I remember them. ‘When he started shouting at me, I would fall on my knees.’”

“He was, by nature, quite honest, and enjoyed his master's full confidence, ever since the time he returned some money his master had lost. So it can be assumed the poor fellow suffered real pangs of remorse at deceiving a master he loved as his benefactor. Severe epileptics, according to the most skilled doctors, are always prone to constant, morbid self-reproach. They agonize over their ‘wickedness,’ they're tormented by pangs of conscience, often entirely without cause; they exaggerate, and often invent, all sorts of faults and crimes. And here we have a man of exactly that type, who really had been driven into wrongdoing by terror and intimidation.”

“He also had a strong premonition that something terrible would come of the situation unfolding before his eyes. When Ivan Fyodorovitch was about to leave for Moscow, just before the catastrophe, Smerdyakov begged him to stay, though he was too timid to say plainly what he feared. He limited himself to hints — hints that went unrecognized.”

“It has to be noted that he regarded Ivan Fyodorovitch as a kind of protector, whose presence in the house guaranteed that nothing bad would happen. Remember the line in Dmitri Karamazov's drunken letter: ‘I'll kill the old man, if only Ivan goes away.’ So Ivan Fyodorovitch's presence seemed, to everyone, a guarantee of peace and order in the house.”

“But he did go away, and within an hour of his young master's departure, Smerdyakov was struck by an epileptic fit. That's easy enough to understand. I should mention here that Smerdyakov, weighed down by a kind of terror and despair, had sensed over those last few days that one of the fits he'd suffered before, at moments of strain, might be coming on again. The exact day and hour of such an attack can't be predicted, of course, but every epileptic can sense beforehand that one is likely. So the doctors tell us. And so, the moment Ivan Fyodorovitch had driven out of the yard, Smerdyakov, weighed down by his lonely, unprotected position, went down to the cellar. As he went down the stairs he was wondering whether he'd have a fit, and what if it struck right then. And that very apprehension, that very wondering, brought on the spasm in his throat that always precedes such attacks, and he fell unconscious into the cellar. And in this perfectly natural occurrence, people try to detect a suspicion — a hint that he faked the attack on purpose. But if it was deliberate, the question arises at once: what was his motive? What was he counting on? What was he aiming for? I'll say nothing about the medicine — science, I'm told, can go astray; the doctors couldn't tell for certain whether it was faked or real. Maybe so. But answer me one question: what motive would he have had for such a fraud? Could he, if he'd been plotting the murder, have wanted to draw the whole household's attention by having a fit right beforehand?”

“You see, gentlemen of the jury, on the night of the murder there were five people at Fyodor Pavlovitch's house — Fyodor Pavlovitch himself (though he obviously didn't kill himself); then his servant Grigory, who was very nearly killed himself; the third was Grigory's wife, Marfa Ignatyevna, though it would be simply shameful to imagine her murdering her master. That leaves two — the prisoner and Smerdyakov. But if we're to believe the prisoner's claim that he isn't the murderer, then it must have been Smerdyakov, since there's no other possibility, no one else to be found. That's what accounts for this cunning, astonishing accusation against the unfortunate feeble-minded man who took his own life yesterday. Had even a shadow of suspicion fallen on anyone else — had there been some sixth person — I'm convinced the prisoner would have been ashamed to accuse Smerdyakov, and would have accused that sixth person instead, because charging Smerdyakov with this murder is simply absurd.”

“Gentlemen, let's set psychology aside, set medicine aside, set even logic aside, and turn only to the facts, to see what they tell us. If Smerdyakov killed him, how did he do it — alone, or with the prisoner's help? Let's consider the first possibility — that he acted alone. If he killed him, he must have had a reason, some advantage for himself. But lacking even a shadow of the motive the prisoner had — hatred, jealousy, and so on — Smerdyakov could only have killed him for money, to get hold of the three thousand roubles he'd seen his master put in the envelope. And yet he tells another person — and a person with the strongest possible stake in it, namely the prisoner — everything about the money, the signals, where the envelope was kept, what was written on it, what it was tied with, and, above all, tells him the very signals that would let him into the house. Did he do this simply to give himself away? Or to invite someone else, someone eager to get that envelope for himself, to join in the plan? ‘Yes,’ I'll be told, ‘but he gave it away out of fear.’ But how do you explain this: a man capable of conceiving such a bold, savage act, and carrying it out, tells someone facts known to no one else on earth — facts that, had he only kept his mouth shut, no one would ever have guessed!”

“No — however much of a coward he might have been, if he'd been plotting such a crime, nothing would have made him tell a soul about the envelope and the signals, because that would have been as good as giving himself away beforehand. He'd have invented something, told some lie if forced to give an account, but he'd have kept quiet about that. Because on the other hand, if he'd said nothing about the money, and had simply committed the murder and stolen the money, no one on earth could have charged him with murder for robbery, since no one but him had ever seen the money, no one but him knew it even existed in the house. Even if he'd been accused of the murder, people could only have supposed he'd committed it for some other motive. But since no one had noticed any such motive in him beforehand, and everyone saw, on the contrary, that his master was fond of him and trusted him, he would, of course, have been the very last person suspected. People would first have suspected the man who had a motive — a man who had openly declared he had such motives, who made no secret of them — in other words, the murdered man's own son, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. If Smerdyakov had killed and robbed him, and the son had been accused of it, that, of course, would have suited Smerdyakov perfectly. And yet are we to believe that, while plotting the murder, he told that very son, Dmitri, about the money, the envelope, and the signals? Is that logical? Does that make any sense?”

“When the day of the murder Smerdyakov is supposed to have planned finally arrived, we find him falling down the stairs in a feigned fit — for what purpose? First, so that Grigory, who had meant to take his medicine, might put it off and stay on guard, seeing there was no one else to watch the house; and second, I suppose, so that his master, seeing there was no one to protect him, and in dread of a visit from his son, might redouble his caution and vigilance. And most of all, I suppose, so that he, Smerdyakov, disabled by the fit, might be carried from the kitchen, where he always slept apart from everyone else and could come and go as he pleased, into Grigory's room at the other end of the lodge, where he was always put whenever he had a fit, shut off by a screen three paces from their own bed. This had been the standing custom, established by his master and the kindhearted Marfa Ignatyevna, every time he had one of his fits. There, lying behind the screen, he most likely, to keep up the pretense, began groaning and kept them both awake all night — as Grigory and his wife testified. And all this, we're meant to believe, so that he could more conveniently get up and murder his master!”

“But I'll be told he faked the illness on purpose to avoid suspicion, and that he told the prisoner about the money and the signals precisely to tempt him into committing the murder — so that once the prisoner had killed him and made off with the money, most likely raising a commotion and waking the household, Smerdyakov got up — am I supposed to believe this? — and went in. For what? To murder his master a second time, and carry off money that had already been stolen? Gentlemen, are you laughing? I'm embarrassed to put forward such a theory, but incredible as it sounds, that's exactly what the prisoner alleges. He tells us that after he left the house, having knocked Grigory down and raised an alarm, Smerdyakov got up, went in, murdered his master, and stole the money! I won't even press the point that Smerdyakov could hardly have counted on any of this beforehand — could hardly have foreseen that the furious, exasperated son, despite knowing the signals, would simply come and peer respectfully through the window and then retreat, leaving Smerdyakov his prize. Gentlemen of the jury, I put this question to you in all seriousness: at what moment could Smerdyakov have committed his crime? Name that moment, or you cannot accuse him.”

“But perhaps, it will be said, the fit was real, and the sick man suddenly came to, heard a shout, and went outside. Well — and then what? He looked around and said to himself, ‘Why not go and kill the master’? And how would he even have known what had happened, since he'd been lying unconscious until that moment? There's a limit to these flights of fancy.”

“‘Quite so,’ some clever people will say to me, ‘but what if they acted together? What if they murdered him jointly and split the money — what then?’ A weighty question, indeed! And the facts backing it up are remarkable. One does the killing and takes all the risk, while his accomplice lies to one side faking a fit, apparently in order to arouse suspicion in everyone — alarm in his master, alarm in Grigory. I'd be curious to know what motive could have driven the two accomplices to hatch such a harebrained scheme.”

“But perhaps it wasn't a case of Smerdyakov actively taking part, but only of passive acquiescence; perhaps Smerdyakov was intimidated and agreed not to stop the murder, and, foreseeing he'd be blamed for letting his master be killed without screaming for help or putting up a fight, obtained permission from Dmitri Karamazov to stay out of the way by faking a fit — ‘murder him however you like, it's nothing to me.’ But since this attack of Smerdyakov's was bound to throw the household into confusion, Dmitri Karamazov could never have agreed to such a plan. I'll set that point aside, though. Suppose he did agree — it would still follow that Dmitri Karamazov is the murderer and the instigator, and Smerdyakov only a passive accomplice, and not even that, but someone who merely went along with it against his will, out of terror.”

“But what do we actually see? The instant he's arrested, the prisoner throws all the blame straight onto Smerdyakov — not accusing him of being his accomplice, but of being the murderer himself. ‘He did it alone,’ he says. ‘He killed him and robbed him. It was his doing.’ Strange sort of accomplices, to start accusing one another right away! And think of the risk for Karamazov. Having committed the murder while his accomplice lay in bed, he pins the blame on the invalid — who might well have resented it, and, to save himself, might well have told the truth. He might well have realized that the court would immediately weigh how far he was responsible, and so he might well have calculated that if he were punished, it would be far less severely than the real murderer. But in that case he would certainly have confessed — and yet he never did. Smerdyakov never once hinted that they'd acted together, even though the actual murderer kept accusing him, insisting he'd committed the crime alone.”

“What's more, at the inquiry Smerdyakov volunteered, on his own, the statement that it was he who had told the prisoner about the envelope of notes and the signals, and that but for him the prisoner would have known nothing about them. If he'd really been a guilty accomplice, would he have offered that statement so readily at the inquiry? On the contrary, he'd have tried to hide it, to twist the facts or play them down. But he did nothing of the kind — he neither twisted nor minimized them. Only an innocent man, with no fear of being charged with complicity, could have behaved as he did. And in a fit of melancholy brought on by his illness and this catastrophe, he hanged himself yesterday. He left behind a note, written in his peculiar language: ‘I destroy myself of my own will and inclination, so as to throw no blame on anyone.’ What would it have cost him to add, ‘I am the murderer, not Karamazov’? But he didn't add that. Did his conscience drive him to suicide, and not to confessing his guilt?”

“And what happened next? Notes for three thousand roubles were brought into court just now, and we were told they were the very ones that had lain in the envelope now sitting on the table before us, and that the witness had received them from Smerdyakov the day before. I won't dwell on that painful scene, though I'll make one or two remarks, choosing trivial ones that might not strike everyone at first glance, and so might get overlooked. First: Smerdyakov must have given back the money and hanged himself out of remorse yesterday. And only yesterday, according to Ivan Karamazov, did he confess his guilt to him. If that weren't so, why would Ivan Fyodorovitch have kept silent until now? So — if he confessed, why, I ask again, didn't he set down the whole truth in the last letter he left behind, knowing full well that the innocent prisoner would have to face this terrible ordeal the very next day?”

“Money alone proves nothing. A week ago, quite by chance, it came to the knowledge of myself and two other people in this courtroom that Ivan Fyodorovitch had sent two five-percent coupon bonds, five thousand each — ten thousand roubles in all — to the provincial capital to be cashed. I mention this only to point out that anyone might have money on hand, and that there's no way to prove these particular notes are the same ones that were in Fyodor Pavlovitch's envelope.”

“Ivan Karamazov, after receiving such an important communication from the real murderer yesterday, did nothing. Why didn't he report it at once? Why did he put it off until morning? I think I have the right to guess why. His health had been failing for a week: he had admitted to a doctor and to his closest friends that he was suffering hallucinations, seeing phantoms of the dead; he was on the brink of the very attack of brain fever that has laid him low today. In that state he suddenly heard of Smerdyakov's death, and at once thought: ‘The man is dead — I can put the blame on him and save my brother. I have money. I'll take a roll of notes and say Smerdyakov gave them to me before he died.’ You'll say that's dishonorable — it's dishonorable to slander even the dead, even to save a brother. True. But what if he slandered him unconsciously? What if, finally unhinged by the sudden news of the valet's death, he genuinely imagined it had happened that way? You saw the scene just now; you saw the state the witness was in. He was standing, he was speaking — but where was his mind?”

“Then came the document — the prisoner's letter, written two days before the crime, laying out a full program for the murder. So why, then, are we looking for any other program? The crime was carried out exactly according to this program, and by no one but the man who wrote it. Yes, gentlemen of the jury — it went off without a hitch! He didn't slink respectfully and timidly away from his father's window, even though he was firmly convinced the object of his affections was with him inside. No — that's absurd, unlikely! He went in, and he murdered him. Most likely he killed him in a rage, burning with resentment the instant he laid eyes on his hated rival. But having killed him — probably with a single blow of the brass pestle — and having made sure, after a careful search, that she wasn't there, he still didn't forget to slip his hand under the pillow and pull out the envelope, whose torn cover now lies on the table before us.”

“I bring up this fact so you'll notice something that strikes me as a very telling detail. Had he been an experienced murderer, and had he committed the murder purely for money, would he have left that torn envelope lying on the floor beside the corpse, right where it was found? Had it been Smerdyakov, say, murdering his master to rob him, he would simply have carried the envelope away with him, without bothering to tear it open over his victim's body, because he'd have known for certain the notes were inside — he'd watched them put in and the envelope sealed. And had he taken the envelope with him, no one would ever have known about the robbery at all. I ask you, gentlemen: would Smerdyakov have behaved that way? Would he have left the envelope on the floor?”

“No — this was the act of a frantic murderer, a murderer who wasn't a thief and had never stolen anything before that day, who snatched the notes from under the pillow not like a thief stealing them, but like a man seizing back his own property from the thief who'd stolen it. Because that was the idea that had become an almost insane obsession for Dmitri Karamazov regarding that money. And pouncing on the envelope, which he'd never laid eyes on before, he tore it open to make sure the money was really there, then ran off with it in his pocket, not even pausing to consider that he'd left behind a devastating piece of evidence against himself in that torn envelope on the floor. All because it was a Karamazov, not a Smerdyakov — he didn't think, didn't stop to reason, and how could he? He ran; he heard the servant cry out behind him; the old man caught up with him, seized him, and was felled to the ground by the brass pestle.”

“The prisoner, moved by pity, jumped down to look at him. Would you believe it — he tells us he jumped down out of pity, out of compassion, to see whether there was anything he could do for him. Was that really a moment for compassion? No — he jumped down simply to find out for certain whether the sole witness to his crime was dead or alive. Any other feeling, any other motive, would be unnatural. Notice that he troubled himself over Grigory, wiped his head with a handkerchief, and, once he'd convinced himself the old man was dead, ran to his mistress's lodgings, dazed and covered in blood. How is it he never once thought he was covered in blood and would be caught at once? But the prisoner himself insists he didn't even notice he was covered in blood. That can be believed — it's entirely possible; that's exactly what happens to criminals at such moments. On one point they'll display diabolical cunning, while another slips past them entirely. But at that moment he was thinking of one thing only — where was she? He wanted to find out at once where she was, so he ran to her lodgings, and there learned an unexpected, astonishing piece of news — she'd gone off to Mokroe to meet her first lover.”

title: IX. The Galloping Troika. The End Of The Prosecutor’s Speech.
paragraphs: Ippolit Kirillovitch had chosen the historical method of presentation, the one so beloved by all nervous speakers, who find in its structure a check on their own overeager rhetoric. At this point in his speech he wandered off into a discussion of Grushenka's “first lover,” and offered up several interesting thoughts on the subject.

“Karamazov, who'd been frantically jealous of every man alive, collapsed, so to speak, and simply gave way before this first lover. What makes it stranger still is that he seems to have hardly given this formidable rival a thought. He'd regarded him as a distant danger, and Karamazov always lives in the present moment. He may even have thought of him as something close to fiction. But his wounded heart understood at once that the woman had been hiding this new rival from him, deceiving him, precisely because the man was anything but fiction to her — because he was the one hope of her life. Grasping this instantly, he gave up.”

“Gentlemen of the jury, I can't help lingering on this unexpected trait in the prisoner's character. He suddenly shows an irresistible longing for fairness, a respect for the woman and a recognition of her right to love — and all this at the very moment when he'd stained his hands with his father's blood for her sake! True, that spilled blood was already crying out for vengeance, because, having ruined his soul and his life in this world, he was forced at that same instant to ask himself what he was, and what he could possibly still be, to her — to that being dearer to him than his own soul — measured against that former lover who had come back, penitent, full of renewed love, to the woman he had once betrayed, bringing honorable proposals and the promise of a reformed, happy life. And what, unlucky man that he was, could he offer her now? What did he have left to give?”

“Karamazov felt all this, knew every path was closed to him by his crime, that he was already a condemned man and not one with a future ahead of him! This thought crushed him. And so he instantly seized on one frantic plan, which, to a man of Karamazov's temperament, must have seemed the only possible way out of his terrible situation. That way out was suicide. He ran for the pistols he'd left in pawn with his friend Perhotin, and on the way, as he ran, he pulled from his pocket the very money for which he'd stained his hands with his father's blood. Oh, now he needed money more than ever. Karamazov was going to die, Karamazov was going to shoot himself — and it would be remembered! To be sure, he was a poet, and had burned the candle at both ends all his life. ‘To her, to her! And there — oh, there I'll throw a feast for the whole world, the likes of which has never been seen, one that will be remembered and talked about for years! In the middle of shouts of wild merriment, reckless gypsy songs and dancing, I'll raise my glass and drink to the woman I adore and to her newfound happiness! And then, right there, at her feet, I'll blow my brains out in front of her and punish myself! She'll remember Mitya Karamazov sometimes — she'll see how Mitya loved her, she'll feel for Mitya!’”

“Here we see, in excess, a taste for grand gestures, romantic despair, sentimentality, and the wild recklessness of the Karamazovs. Yes — but there's something else, gentlemen of the jury, something that cries out in the soul, throbs ceaselessly in the mind, and poisons the heart to the point of death — that something is conscience, gentlemen of the jury, its verdict, its terrible torments! The pistol will settle everything — the pistol is the only way out! But beyond — I don't know whether Karamazov, at that moment, wondered ‘what lies beyond,’ whether Karamazov could, like Hamlet, wonder ‘what lies beyond.’ No, gentlemen of the jury — they have their Hamlets, but we still have only our Karamazovs!”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch painted a detailed picture of Mitya's preparations — the scene at Perhotin's, at the shop, with the drivers. He quoted numerous words and actions, all confirmed by witnesses, and the picture made a terrible impression on the audience. The guilt of this harried, desperate man stood out clear and convincing once all the facts were laid side by side.

“What need did he have for caution? Two or three times he very nearly confessed, hinted at it, all but came out and said it.” (Then followed the testimony given by witnesses.) “He even shouted at the peasant driving him, ‘Do you know you're driving a murderer!’ But it was impossible for him to come out and say it — he had to reach Mokroe and finish his romance there. But what was waiting for the unlucky man? Almost from the first minute at Mokroe he saw that his invincible rival was perhaps nothing of the kind, that the toast to their newfound happiness was neither wanted nor welcome. But you already know the facts, gentlemen of the jury, from the preliminary inquiry. Karamazov's triumph over his rival was total, and his soul passed into an entirely new phase — perhaps the most terrible phase his soul has ever passed through, or ever will.”

“One can say with certainty, gentlemen of the jury,” the prosecutor went on, “that outraged nature and a guilty heart exact their own vengeance more thoroughly than any earthly justice ever could. What's more, justice and punishment here on earth actually ease the punishment of nature, and are indeed essential to the criminal soul in such moments, as its rescue from despair. Because I can't even imagine the horror, the moral agony, Karamazov must have felt on learning that she loved him — that for his sake she had turned away her first lover, that she was calling him, Mitya, to a new life, promising him happiness — and when? When it was all over for him, when nothing was possible anymore!”

“By the way, I'll note in passing a point of some importance, for the light it throws on the prisoner's state of mind at the time. This woman, the object of his love, had been, right up until the last moment — right up to the instant of his arrest — a being unattainable, passionately desired, and out of reach. Yet why didn't he shoot himself then? Why did he abandon his plan, and even forget where his pistol was? It was precisely that passionate longing for love, and the hope of finally satisfying it, that held him back. All through the revels he stayed close beside his adored mistress, who was there at the feast with him and more charming, more captivating to him than ever — he never left her side, abasing himself before her in worship.”

“His passion might well, for a moment, have stifled not only his fear of arrest but even the torments of conscience. For a moment — oh, only for a moment! I can picture the state of mind of a criminal hopelessly enslaved by these forces — first, the influence of drink, of noise and excitement, of the thud of the dancing and the wail of the singing, and of her, flushed with wine, singing and dancing and laughing at him! Second, the lingering hope that the fatal reckoning might still be far off — that they wouldn't come for him until the next morning at the very earliest. So he had a few hours, and that's a great deal — a very great deal! In a few hours a man can think of many things. I imagine he felt something like what condemned men feel on their way to the scaffold. There's still a long, long street left to cross, walking at a measured pace, past thousands of people. Then there'll be a turn into another street, and only at the far end of that one, the dreaded place of execution! I fancy that at the start of the journey, the condemned man, sitting on his cart of shame, must feel he still has a whole lifetime ahead of him. The houses fall away behind, the cart rolls on — oh, that's nothing, there's still a long way to the turn into the second street, and he still looks boldly to right and left at those thousands of coldly curious people with their eyes fixed on him, and still imagines he's just such a man as they are. But now comes the turn into the next street. Oh, that's nothing, nothing — there's still a whole street ahead of him, and however many houses he's passed already, he'll still believe plenty remain. And so on, all the way to the very scaffold.”

“This, I imagine, is how it was with Karamazov then. ‘They haven't had time yet,’ he must have thought. ‘I might still find a way out — oh, there's still time to think of some defense, and right now, right now — she's so captivating!’”

“His soul was in turmoil and dread, and yet he still managed to set aside half his money and hide it somewhere — I can find no other explanation for the disappearance of fully half the three thousand he'd just taken from under his father's pillow. He'd been to Mokroe more than once before, had spent two whole days carousing there already, and knew every passage and outbuilding of the big old house. My guess is that part of the money was hidden somewhere in that house, not long before his arrest — in some crevice, under some floorboard, in some corner, under the roof. To what end, I'll be asked? Well — the catastrophe might strike at any moment, of course; he hadn't yet worked out how to face it, hadn't had the time, his head was pounding and his heart was with her — but money, money was essential no matter what. With money, a man is always still a man. Perhaps such foresight, at such a moment, strikes you as unnatural? But he assures us himself that a month earlier, at a tense and critical moment, he'd halved his money and sewn it into a little bag. And though that wasn't true, as we'll prove directly, it shows the idea was a familiar one to Karamazov — he'd already considered it. What's more, when he declared at the inquiry that he'd put fifteen hundred roubles in a bag (a bag that never existed), he may well have invented that little bag on the spur of the moment, precisely because two hours earlier he actually had divided his money and hidden half of it at Mokroe until morning, in case of emergency, simply so as not to be carrying it on him. Two extremes, gentlemen of the jury — remember that a Karamazov can hold two extremes in mind at once, and both together.”

“We searched the house, but found no money. It may still be there, or it may have vanished the next day and be in the prisoner's hands even now. In any case, he was at her side, on his knees before her — she lay on the bed, he stretched his hands out to her, and he had so completely forgotten everything else that he didn't even hear the men come to arrest him. He hadn't had time to prepare any line of defense. He was caught off guard, unprepared, and brought face to face with his judges, the arbiters of his fate.”

“Gentlemen of the jury, there are moments in the carrying out of our duties when it's a terrible thing to face a man — terrible for him too. The moments of watching that animal fear, when the criminal sees that everything is lost, but still struggles, still means to go on struggling, when every instinct of self-preservation rises up in him at once and he looks at you with pleading, suffering eyes, studying you, your face, your thoughts, unsure which way you'll strike, his distracted mind spinning out a thousand plans in an instant, and yet still afraid to speak, afraid of giving himself away! This purgatory of the spirit, this animal thirst for self-preservation, these humiliating moments of the human soul, are terrible to watch, and can rouse horror and pity for the criminal even in a lawyer. And this is exactly what we all witnessed that night.”

“At first he was thunderstruck, and in his terror let slip a few deeply incriminating words. ‘Blood! I've earned it!’ But he quickly caught himself. He hadn't prepared what he was going to say, what answer he'd give — he had nothing ready but a flat denial. ‘I'm not guilty of my father's death.’ That was his line of defense for the moment, and behind it he hoped to throw up some sort of barricade. His first damaging outbursts he hurried to explain away, insisting he was responsible only for the servant Grigory's death. ‘For that bloodshed, yes, I'm guilty — but who killed my father, gentlemen, who killed him? Who could have killed him, if not I?’ Do you hear that — he asked us that, us, the very people who'd come to ask him that question! Do you hear that phrase, blurted out with such premature haste — ‘if not I’ — the animal cunning in it, the naïveté, the Karamazov impatience? ‘I didn't kill him, and you mustn't think I did! I wanted to kill him, gentlemen, I wanted to,’ he rushes to admit (he was in a hurry, a terrible hurry), ‘but still, I'm not guilty — it wasn't I who murdered him.’ He concedes to us that he wanted to murder him, as if to say: you see for yourselves how truthful I am, so you'll believe all the more readily that I didn't murder him. Oh, in such cases the criminal is often astonishingly shallow and credulous.”

“At that point one of the lawyers asked him, almost casually, the simplest possible question: ‘Wasn't it Smerdyakov who killed him?’ Then, just as we expected, he grew furious that we'd anticipated him and caught him off guard, before he'd had time to prepare his ground, to pick and choose the moment when it would seem most natural to bring Smerdyakov's name up. He immediately swung to the opposite extreme, as he always does, and began insisting that Smerdyakov couldn't have killed him, wasn't capable of it. But don't believe him — that was only his cunning; he hadn't really given up on Smerdyakov at all; on the contrary, he meant to bring him forward again, because he had no one else to offer, but he'd do it later, since for the moment that line had been spoiled for him. He'd bring him up, perhaps, the next day, or even some days later, waiting for the right moment to cry out to us, ‘You know, I was more skeptical about Smerdyakov than any of you — you remember that yourselves — but now I'm convinced. He killed him, he must have!’ And for the time being he falls back on a sullen, irritable denial. Impatience and anger, though, drove him into the most clumsy, incredible explanation of how he'd looked in at his father's window and then respectfully withdrawn. The worst of it was that he didn't yet know how things stood — didn't know what Grigory had testified.”

“We proceeded to search him. The search angered him, but also, oddly, encouraged him — the full three thousand wasn't found on him, only half of it. And no doubt it was precisely in that moment of angry silence that the fiction of the little bag first occurred to him. No doubt he was aware himself of how implausible the story sounded, and struggled painfully to make it more convincing, to weave it into a plausible-sounding tale. In cases like this, the first duty, the chief task of the examining lawyers, is to keep the criminal from preparing himself — to catch him off guard, so that he blurts out his cherished ideas in all their raw simplicity, improbability, and inconsistency. The only way to get a criminal talking is through the sudden, apparently offhand disclosure of some new fact, some circumstance of real importance to the case, one he had no idea of and couldn't have foreseen. We had just such a fact ready — Grigory's testimony about the open door the prisoner had run out through. He had completely forgotten about that door, hadn't even suspected Grigory could have seen it.”

“The effect was extraordinary. He leapt up and shouted at us, ‘Then it was Smerdyakov who murdered him — it was Smerdyakov!’ — and in doing so gave away the very defense he'd been holding in reserve, and gave it away in its most implausible form, since Smerdyakov could only have committed the murder after the prisoner had already knocked Grigory down and fled. When we told him that Grigory had seen the door open before he fell, and had heard Smerdyakov behind the screen as he came out of his bedroom, Karamazov was utterly crushed. My esteemed and witty colleague, Nikolay Parfenovitch, told me afterward that he was almost moved to tears at the sight of him. And to make matters worse, the prisoner hurried to tell us about the now-famous little bag — very well, then, you shall hear this romance!”

“Gentlemen of the jury, I've already told you why I consider this romance not merely absurd, but the single most improbable invention that could possibly have been put forward under the circumstances. If you tried, for a bet, to invent the least believable story imaginable, you'd have a hard time finding anything more incredible. The trouble with such stories is that the storytellers, so pleased with themselves, are always tripped up and undone by exactly the details in which real life is so rich, and which these unlucky, involuntary novelists overlook as insignificant trifles. Oh, they have no attention to spare for such details — their minds are fixed on their grand invention as a whole, and imagine anyone daring to pull them up over something so small! But that's precisely how they're caught. The prisoner was asked: ‘Where did you get the material for your little bag, and who sewed it?’ ‘I made it myself.’ ‘And where did you get the linen?’ The prisoner was actually offended — he found it almost insulting to be asked such a trivial question, and, believe it or not, his resentment was genuine! But they're all like that. ‘I tore it off my shirt.’ ‘Then we'll find that shirt among your linen tomorrow, with a piece torn off it.’ And just imagine, gentlemen of the jury, if we really had found that torn shirt (and how could we possibly have failed to, in his chest of drawers or his trunk?) — that would have been a fact, a solid fact supporting his account! But he was incapable of that kind of reflection. ‘I don't remember — maybe it wasn't off my shirt. I sewed it into one of my landlady's caps.’ ‘What kind of cap?’ ‘It was an old cotton rag of hers, lying around.’ ‘And you remember that clearly?’ ‘No, I don't.’ And he was angry, very angry — and yet, imagine, not remembering it! At the most terrible moments of a man's life — say, when he's being led to execution — he remembers precisely such trifles. He'll forget everything except some green roof flashing past on the road, or a jackdaw perched on a cross — that he'll remember. He hid the making of that little bag from his household; he must have remembered his humiliating fear that someone might come in and find him with a needle in his hand, how at the slightest sound he'd duck behind the screen (there is a screen in his lodgings).”

“But, gentlemen of the jury, why am I telling you all this — all these details, these trifles?” Ippolit Kirillovitch suddenly cried. “Simply because the prisoner still clings to these absurdities to this very moment. He hasn't explained a single thing since that fatal night two months ago; he hasn't added one genuinely illuminating fact to his earlier fantastic claims — it's all trivialities. ‘You must take my word of honor for it.’ Oh, we'd be glad to believe it — eager to believe it, even on his word of honor alone! Are we jackals, thirsting for human blood? Show us a single fact in the prisoner's favor and we'll rejoice — but let it be a solid, real fact, not some inference drawn by his own brother from the look on his face, or from the idea that when he beat his chest he must have meant to point at the little bag, and in the dark, no less. We'll welcome any new fact — we'll be the first to withdraw our charge, we'll hurry to withdraw it. But as things stand, justice cries out, and we hold firm — we can withdraw nothing.”

Ippolit Kirillovitch moved into his final peroration. He looked feverish; he spoke of the blood crying out for vengeance, the blood of a father murdered by his own son for the base motive of robbery! He pointed to the tragic, glaring consistency of the facts.

“And whatever you may hear from the talented, celebrated counsel for the defense,” Ippolit Kirillovitch couldn't resist adding, “whatever eloquent, moving appeals may be made to your feelings, remember that at this moment you stand in a temple of justice. Remember that you are the champions of our justice, the champions of our holy Russia, of her principles, her family, everything she holds sacred! Yes — at this moment you stand here for Russia, and your verdict will echo not only through this hall but across the whole of Russia, and all Russia will hear you as her champions and her judges, and she will take heart or lose heart according to your verdict. Do not disappoint Russia and her hopes. Our fatal troika races on in its headlong flight, perhaps toward destruction, and for a long time now, throughout Russia, men have stretched out imploring hands, calling for a halt to its furious, reckless course. And if other nations step aside from that troika, it may not be out of respect, as the poet would have us believe, but simply out of horror — of horror, perhaps of disgust. And it's well that they step aside; but perhaps one day they will stop doing so, and will form a solid wall against the rushing apparition, and will check the frenzied rush of our lawlessness, for the sake of their own safety, their own enlightenment, their own civilization. Already we hear voices of alarm coming from Europe — they're already beginning to sound. Do not tempt them! Do not add to their growing hatred with a verdict that justifies a son murdering his father!”

Though Ippolit Kirillovitch was genuinely moved, he closed his speech with this rhetorical flourish, and its effect on the audience was extraordinary. When he'd finished, he hurried out and, as I've already mentioned, very nearly fainted in the next room. There was no applause in the courtroom, but the more serious-minded people were pleased. The ladies were less satisfied, though even they admired his eloquence, especially since they felt no real anxiety about the trial's outcome and had full confidence in Fetyukovitch. ‘He'll speak at last, and of course he'll carry everything before him.’

Everyone was looking at Mitya; he sat silent through the whole of the prosecutor's speech, teeth clenched, hands clasped, head bowed. Only now and then he raised his head to listen, especially whenever Grushenka was mentioned. When the prosecutor brought up Rakitin's opinion of her, a look of contempt and anger crossed his face, and he muttered, quite audibly, ‘The Bernards!’ When Ippolit Kirillovitch described how he'd been questioned and tormented at Mokroe, Mitya raised his head and listened with fierce curiosity. At one point he looked ready to jump up and shout something, but he controlled himself and only shrugged his shoulders in disdain. People talked afterward about the end of the speech, about the prosecutor's feat of cross-examining the prisoner at Mokroe, and made fun of Ippolit Kirillovitch. ‘The man couldn't help boasting about his own cleverness,’ they said.
