The court adjourned, but only for a short break — a quarter of an hour, twenty minutes at most. There was a buzz of conversation and exclamations throughout the audience. I remember a few of them.
“A weighty speech,” a gentleman in one group observed gravely.
“He brought in too much psychology,” said another voice.
“But it was all true — the plain truth!”
“Yes, he's first-rate at that.”
“He summed it all up.”
“Yes, he summed us up too,” chimed in another voice. “Do you remember, right at the start of his speech, making it sound like we're all like Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“And at the end, too. But that was all nonsense.”
“And obscure, too.”
“He got a little carried away.”
“It's unfair — it's unfair.”
“No, it was cleverly done, all the same. He's had to wait a long time, but he's had his say — ha ha!”
“What will the counsel for the defense say?”
In another group I overheard:
“He shouldn't have taken a jab at the Petersburg man like that — ‘appealing to your sensibilities,’ do you remember?”
“Yes, that was clumsy of him.”
“He was in too much of a hurry.”
“He's a nervous man.”
“We laugh, but what must the prisoner be feeling right now?”
“Yes — what must it be like for Mitya?”
In a third group:
“Who's that lady, the heavyset one with the lorgnette, sitting at the end?”
“A general's wife, divorced — I know her.”
“That's why she has the lorgnette.”
“She's not much to look at.”
“Oh, no — she's quite a piquant little woman.”
“Two seats past her there's a small fair-haired woman — she's prettier.”
“They caught him neatly at Mokroe, didn't they, eh?”
“Oh, it was clever enough. We've heard it all before — how many times has he told the story at people's houses!”
“And he couldn't resist doing it again now. That's vanity.”
“He's a man with a grievance, heh heh!”
“Yes, and quick to take offense. And too much rhetoric — such long sentences.”
“Yes, he's trying to scare us, he kept trying to scare us. Do you remember that bit about the troika? Something like, ‘They have Hamlets, but so far we only have Karamazovs!’ That was clever, that.”
“That was to win over the liberals. He's afraid of them.”
“Yes, and he's afraid of the lawyer too.”
“Yes — what will Fetyukovitch say?”
“Whatever he says, he won't win over our peasants.”
“You don't think so?”
A fourth group:
“That bit he said about the troika was good — that part about the other nations.”
“And it was true, what he said about other nations not putting up with it.”
“What do you mean?”

“Well — a member of the English Parliament got up last week, talking about the Nihilists, and asked the ministry whether it wasn't high time to step in, to civilize this barbarous people. Ippolit had him in mind, I know he did. He was talking about it just last week.”
“Not an easy job.”
“Not an easy job? Why not?”
“Well, we'd close off Kronstadt and cut off their grain. Where would they get it from?”
“From America. They get it from America now.”
“Nonsense!”
But the bell rang, and everyone rushed back to their seats. Fetyukovitch mounted the tribune.

title: X. The Speech For The Defense. An Argument That Cuts Both Ways
paragraphs: All was hushed as the first words of the famous orator rang out. Every eye in the room fixed on him. He began very simply, very directly, with an air of conviction but not a trace of conceit. He made no attempt at eloquence, at pathos, at emotional phrase-making. He spoke like a man addressing a circle of close, sympathetic friends. His voice was a fine one — sonorous, warm — and there was something genuine and simple in its very sound. But everyone sensed at once that this speaker might suddenly rise to real pathos and “pierce the heart with untold power.” His language was, if anything, less regular than Ippolit Kirillovitch's, but he avoided long sentences, and in fact spoke with greater precision. One thing displeased the ladies: he kept bending forward, especially at the start of his speech — not quite a bow, more as though he were about to lunge at his listeners, folding his long spine almost in half, as if there were a spring at its center that let him bend nearly at a right angle.

At the start of his speech he spoke rather disjointedly, without much order, you might say — handling facts one at a time — though by the end they came together into a whole. His speech could be divided into two parts: the first, criticism refuting the charge, at times bitter and sarcastic. But in the second half he suddenly changed his tone, even his manner, and rose at once to pathos. The audience seemed to have been waiting for it, and trembled with enthusiasm.

He got straight to the point, opening by saying that although his practice was in Petersburg, he had more than once traveled to provincial towns to defend prisoners of whose innocence he was convinced, or at least had formed a strong preliminary impression. “That's what's happened to me in the present case,” he explained. “From the very first newspaper reports, something struck me that strongly predisposed me in the prisoner's favor. What interested me most was a fact that comes up often enough in legal practice, but rarely, I think, in such an extreme and peculiar form as here. I ought by rights to save this peculiarity for the end of my speech, but I'll state it right at the start, because it's a weakness of mine to get straight to work, rather than holding my effects in reserve and rationing my material. That may be imprudent of me, but at least it's honest. Here is what I have in mind: there is an overwhelming chain of evidence against the prisoner, and yet not one single fact in that chain will hold up to scrutiny if examined on its own. The more closely I followed the case in the papers, the more this idea was confirmed, and then, suddenly, I received a request from the prisoner's family to take on his defense. I hurried here at once, and once here, became fully convinced. It was in order to break apart this terrible chain of facts, to show that each piece of evidence, taken on its own, is unproven and fanciful, that I took the case.”
So Fetyukovitch began.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” he suddenly said, “I am new to this district. I have no preconceptions. The prisoner, a man of turbulent, unbridled temper, has never insulted me personally. But he has, perhaps, insulted hundreds of people in this town, and so turned many of them against him in advance. Of course I recognize that local opinion has been justly roused against him. The prisoner is turbulent, violent by temperament. And yet he was received in society here — he was even a welcome guest in the household of my talented friend, the prosecutor.”

(N.B. At these words there were two or three bursts of laughter in the audience, quickly stifled but noticed by everyone. We all knew the prosecutor had received Mitya against his own wishes, purely because Mitya had somehow interested his wife — a lady of the highest virtue and moral character, but fanciful, headstrong, and fond of crossing her husband, especially in small things. Mitya's visits, however, had not been frequent.)

“And yet I venture to suggest,” Fetyukovitch went on, “that despite his independence of mind and his upright character, my opponent may have formed a mistaken prejudice against my unfortunate client. Oh, that's only natural — the poor man has all too thoroughly earned such prejudice. Outraged morality, and outraged taste even more, are often merciless. In the talented prosecutor's speech we heard a severe analysis of the prisoner's character and conduct; his rigorous, critical stance on the case was plain throughout. What's more, he ventured into psychological subtleties he couldn't possibly have entered into had he held even the slightest conscious, malicious bias against the prisoner. But there are things worse, even more damaging in cases like this, than the most consciously malicious, unfair attitude. It's worse when we're carried away by artistic instinct, by the urge to build, so to speak, a novel — especially when God has blessed us with a gift for psychological insight. Before I set out for this town, I was warned in Petersburg, and I already knew myself, that I would find here a talented opponent whose psychological insight and subtlety have earned him particular renown in legal circles these past few years. But however deep psychology may run, it's a knife that cuts both ways.” (Laughter in the courtroom.) “You'll forgive the comparison, of course — I can't claim eloquence. But let me take, as an example, any point from the prosecutor's speech.”

“The prisoner, fleeing through the dark garden, climbed over the fence, was seized by the servant, and knocked him down with a brass pestle. Then he jumped back into the garden and spent five whole minutes over the man, trying to work out whether he'd killed him or not. And the prosecutor refuses to believe the prisoner's statement that he ran back to old Grigory out of pity. ‘No,’ he says, ‘such tenderness is impossible at a moment like that — it's unnatural. He ran back to find out whether the only witness to his crime was dead or alive, and in doing so proved he'd committed the murder, since he'd have had no other reason to run back.’”

“There you have psychology — but let's take that same method and apply it the other way around, and we'll get a result no less plausible. We're told the murderer jumped down as a precaution, to check whether the witness was alive or dead, and yet he'd left behind, in his murdered father's study, as the prosecutor himself points out, a remarkable piece of evidence — a torn envelope, with an inscription stating there had once been three thousand roubles inside it. ‘Had he carried that envelope off with him, no one on earth would ever have known about the envelope, or about the money in it, or that the prisoner had stolen it.’ Those are the prosecutor's own words. So on one side you have a total absence of caution — a man who's lost his head and fled in a panic, leaving that piece of evidence on the floor — and then, two minutes later, having just killed another man, we're supposed to credit him with the coldest, most calculating foresight imaginable. But even granting that this was so, I suppose it takes real psychological subtlety to discover that under certain circumstances I become as bloodthirsty and sharp-eyed as a Caucasian eagle, while the very next moment I'm as timid and blind as a mole. But if I'm so bloodthirsty and coldly calculating that after killing a man I only run back to check whether he's alive to testify against me, why would I then spend five minutes hovering over my victim, at the risk of running into other witnesses? Why soak my handkerchief wiping the blood off his head, so it can later be used as evidence against me? If he was really so cold and calculating, why not strike the servant on the head again and again with the same pestle, to finish him off outright and be done with all that anxiety about a witness?”

“And again — though he ran back to check whether the witness was alive, he left another witness lying right on the path: that brass pestle, taken from the two women, which they could always identify afterward as theirs and use to prove he'd taken it from them. And it's not as though he simply forgot it on the path, dropped it through carelessness or haste — no, he flung the weapon away, since it was found fifteen paces from where Grigory lay. Why did he do that? Simply because he was grieved at having killed a man — an old servant — and he hurled the pestle away with a curse, as a murder weapon. That's surely how it must have happened — what other reason could he have had for throwing it so far? And if he was capable of feeling grief and pity at having killed a man, that shows he was innocent of his father's murder. Had he actually murdered his father, he would never have run to help another victim out of pity — he would have felt very differently then; his thoughts would have been fixed entirely on self-preservation, with none to spare for pity — that much is beyond doubt. On the contrary, he'd have cracked the man's skull rather than spend five minutes tending to him. There was room for pity and good feeling precisely because his conscience had been clear up to that point. Here we have an altogether different psychology. I've resorted to this method on purpose, gentlemen of the jury, to show you that it can prove anything at all. It all depends on who's wielding it. Psychology can lure even the most serious people into pure invention, quite without their realizing it. I'm speaking of the abuse of psychology, gentlemen.”

Sounds of approval and laughter, this time at the prosecutor's expense, were heard again in the courtroom. I won't repeat the speech in full; I'll only quote a few passages from it, a few of its main points.

title: XI. There Was No Money. There Was No Robbery
paragraphs: There was one point in Fetyukovitch's speech that struck everyone. He flatly denied the existence of the fatal three thousand roubles, and consequently, the very possibility that it had ever been stolen.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” he began. “Any new, unbiased observer is bound to be struck by a peculiar feature of this case — namely, the charge of robbery, combined with the complete impossibility of proving there was ever anything to steal. We're told money was stolen — three thousand roubles — but whether that sum ever existed, nobody actually knows. Consider: how have we even heard of this sum, and who has ever laid eyes on the notes? The only person who saw them, and claimed they'd been placed in the envelope, was the servant Smerdyakov. He'd mentioned it to the prisoner and to his brother, Ivan Fyodorovitch, before the catastrophe. Madame Svyetlov, too, had been told of it. But not one of these three people ever actually saw the notes — only Smerdyakov did.”

“And here a question arises: if it's true they existed, and that Smerdyakov saw them, when did he last see them? What if his master had taken the notes out from under his mattress and put them back in his cash box without telling him? Note that, according to Smerdyakov's own account, the notes were kept under the mattress — the prisoner must have pulled them out from there — and yet the bed was found completely undisturbed, a fact carefully recorded in the official record. How could the prisoner have found the notes without disturbing the bed at all? How could he have avoided staining, with his bloodied hands, the fine, spotless linen on that carefully made bed?”

“But I'll be asked: what about the envelope on the floor? Yes, that envelope deserves a word or two. I was rather surprised to hear the highly talented prosecutor declare — of himself, mind you — that if that envelope hadn't been left on the floor, no one on earth would ever have known that it, or the notes inside it, existed, and therefore that the prisoner had stolen it. So, by the prosecutor's own admission, that torn scrap of paper is the sole piece of evidence on which the entire charge of robbery rests — ‘otherwise no one would have known of the robbery, or perhaps even of the money at all.’ But does the simple fact that this scrap of paper was lying on the floor actually prove there had been money inside it, and that this money had been stolen? Yes, I'll be told, but Smerdyakov had seen the money in the envelope. But when — when had he last seen it, I ask you? I spoke with Smerdyakov myself, and he told me he'd last seen the notes two days before the catastrophe. Then why not consider the possibility that old Fyodor Pavlovitch, shut up alone in feverish, impatient anticipation of the object of his adoration, whiled away the time by tearing open the envelope and taking out the notes? ‘What's the use of the envelope?’ he may have thought to himself. ‘She won't believe the money's really there — but if I show her all thirty rainbow-colored notes rolled up in one bundle, that'll make a much stronger impression, you can be sure — it'll make her mouth water.’ And so he tears the envelope open, takes out the money, and tosses the envelope on the floor, quite unbothered, feeling himself the sole owner, with no thought of leaving evidence behind.”

“Listen, gentlemen — could anything be more plausible than this theory, this course of events? Why should it be out of the question? But if something of the kind could have happened, then the whole charge of robbery collapses; if there was no money, then there was no theft of it. If the envelope on the floor can be taken as evidence that there was once money in it, why can't I just as well argue the opposite — that the envelope was on the floor precisely because its owner had already taken the money out of it?”

“But I'll be asked what became of the money, if Fyodor Pavlovitch had taken it out of the envelope, since it was never found when the police searched the house. In the first place, part of the money was found in the cash box; and in the second, he may have taken it out that very morning, or the evening before, to put it to some other use — to give it away, or send it somewhere — he may have changed his plans entirely, without feeling any need to announce as much to Smerdyakov beforehand. And if there's even the barest possibility of such an explanation, how can the prisoner be so confidently accused of having committed murder for robbery, and of actually carrying out that robbery? This strays into the territory of pure invention. If it's claimed that something was stolen, the thing itself must be produced, or at least its existence must be proven beyond doubt. Yet no one has ever laid eyes on these notes.”

“Not long ago in Petersburg, an eighteen-year-old — hardly more than a boy — who made his living as a small-time street peddler, walked in broad daylight into a moneychanger's shop with an axe, and with extraordinary, almost textbook boldness, killed the shop's owner and made off with fifteen hundred roubles. Five hours later he was arrested, and, apart from the fifteen roubles he'd already managed to spend, the entire sum was found on him. What's more, when the shop assistant returned after the murder, he was able to tell the police not only the exact amount stolen but even the specific notes and coins that made up that sum — and those very notes and coins were found on the criminal. This was followed by a full, genuine confession from the murderer. That, gentlemen of the jury, is what I call evidence! There, I know, I see, I can touch the money — I can't deny it exists. Is it the same in this case? And yet it's a matter of life and death.”

“Yes, I'll be told, but he was out carousing that night, throwing money around — he was shown to have had fifteen hundred roubles on him — where did he get it? But the very fact that only fifteen hundred could be found, and the other half of the sum could nowhere be located, shows that this money wasn't the same money, and had never been in any envelope at all. It was proved at the preliminary inquiry, by a strict accounting of the timeline, that the prisoner ran straight from the two women servants to Perhotin's without going home first, and hadn't been anywhere else. So he'd been in company the entire time, and couldn't possibly have split the three thousand in half and hidden half of it somewhere in town. It's precisely this consideration that led the prosecutor to suppose the money is hidden in some crevice at Mokroe. Why not in the dungeons of the castle of Udolpho, gentlemen? Isn't this supposition really far too fanciful, far too much like a novel? And notice — if that supposition falls apart, the entire charge of robbery scatters to the winds, because in that case, what could have become of the other fifteen hundred roubles? By what miracle could they have vanished, given that it's been proven the prisoner went nowhere else? And we're prepared to ruin a man's life on the strength of stories like these!”

“I'll be told he couldn't explain where he got the fifteen hundred he had, and that everyone knew he was penniless before that night. Who knew it, exactly? The prisoner has given a clear, consistent account of where that money came from, and if you'll allow it, gentlemen of the jury, nothing could be more plausible than that account, or more in keeping with the prisoner's character and temperament. The prosecutor is enchanted with his own invention. A weak-willed man, we're told, who'd brought himself to accept the three thousand so insultingly offered by his betrothed, couldn't possibly have set half of it aside and sewn it up — and even if he had, he'd have unpicked it every couple of days to take out a hundred at a time, and would have spent the whole lot within a month. All this, you'll recall, was delivered in a tone that brooked no argument. But what if things happened quite differently? What if you've been spinning a novel — about an entirely different sort of man? That's exactly it — you've invented an entirely different man!”

“I'll be told, perhaps, that there are witnesses who saw him spend, in a single day, the whole three thousand given him by his betrothed a month before the catastrophe — so he couldn't possibly have split the sum in half. But who are these witnesses? The value of their testimony has already been shown in this courtroom. Besides, in another man's hand a piece of bread always looks bigger, and not one of these witnesses actually counted that money — they simply judged by eye. And the witness Maximov testified that the prisoner had twenty thousand roubles in his hand. You see, gentlemen of the jury, psychology cuts both ways. Let me turn the blade the other direction now, and see what comes of it.”

“A month before the catastrophe, the prisoner was entrusted by Katerina Ivanovna with three thousand roubles to send off by post. But the question is: is it really true that it was handed over to him in such an insulting, degrading way as was just proclaimed here? The young lady's first account of the matter was different — entirely different. In her second account we heard nothing but cries of resentment and revenge, cries of long-suppressed hatred. And the very fact that the witness gave incorrect testimony the first time gives us every right to suspect her second account may have been incorrect as well. The prosecutor will not, dares not (his own words), touch on that story. Very well — I won't touch on it either, but I will venture to observe that if a high-principled, noble person — and that highly respected young lady is unquestionably such a person — allows herself suddenly, in open court, to contradict her own earlier statement, with the obvious aim of ruining the prisoner, it's clear that this testimony was not given impartially, not calmly. Don't we have the right to assume that a vengeful woman might have exaggerated a great deal? Yes — she may well have exaggerated, in particular, the insult and humiliation involved in offering him the money. No — it was offered in a way that made it possible to accept, especially for a man as easygoing as the prisoner, above all because he expected to receive from his father, very soon, the three thousand roubles he believed was owed to him. It was reckless of him, but it was exactly this reckless lack of reflection that made him so confident his father would give him the money, that he'd get it, and so he'd always be able to send off the sum entrusted to him and repay the debt.”

“But the prosecutor won't allow that he could have set aside half the money that same day and sewn it into a little bag. That's not in his character, we're told — he couldn't have had such feelings. And yet the prosecutor himself spoke of the broad Karamazov nature; he cried out about the two extremes a Karamazov can hold in mind at once. Karamazov is exactly that kind of two-sided nature, swinging between two extremes — so that even when gripped by the most violent craving for riotous pleasure, he can pull himself up short if something strikes him from the other direction. And on the other side was love — that new love that had flared up in his heart, and for that love he needed money, oh, far more than for carousing with his mistress. If she'd said to him, ‘I am yours, I won't have Fyodor Pavlovitch,’ then he'd have needed money to take her away. That mattered more than any carousing. Could a Karamazov fail to understand that? That anxiety was precisely what he was suffering from — what's so improbable about his setting that money aside, hiding it against an emergency?”

“But time went by, and Fyodor Pavlovitch never gave the prisoner the three thousand he was expecting; on the contrary, he heard that his father meant to use that very sum to lure away the woman he, the prisoner, loved. ‘If Fyodor Pavlovitch won't give me the money,’ he thought, ‘I'll be exposed as a thief before Katerina Ivanovna.’ And then it occurred to him that he could go to Katerina Ivanovna, lay before her the fifteen hundred roubles he still carried around his neck, and say, ‘I'm a scoundrel, but not a thief.’ So here we already have two reasons why he would guard that sum like the apple of his eye, why he wouldn't unpick the little bag and spend it a hundred at a time. Why should we deny the prisoner a sense of honor? Yes, he has one — granted it's misplaced, granted it's often mistaken — and yet it exists, and amounts to something like a passion, and he's proven as much.”

“But now the matter grows even more complicated: his jealous torments reach a peak, and those same two questions gnaw more and more at his fevered mind: ‘If I pay back Katerina Ivanovna, where will I find the means to run off with Grushenka?’ If he behaved wildly that month, drank, made scenes in taverns, it was perhaps because he was miserable and strained past the limits of his endurance. These two questions became so acute that they finally drove him to despair. He sent his younger brother to beg his father, one last time, for the three thousand roubles, but without waiting for an answer, burst in himself and ended by beating the old man in front of witnesses. After that he had no hope of getting the money from anyone; his father certainly wasn't going to give it to him after that beating.”

“That same evening he struck himself on the chest, right on the upper part where the little bag was, and swore to his brother that he had the means not to be a scoundrel — but that he would remain a scoundrel all the same, because he already foresaw he wouldn't use those means, that he lacked the character, the willpower, to do it. Why, why does the prosecutor refuse to believe Alexey Karamazov's testimony, given so genuinely and sincerely, so spontaneously and convincingly? And why, instead, does he force me to believe in money hidden in some crevice, in the dungeons of the castle of Udolpho?”

“That same evening, after his talk with his brother, the prisoner wrote that fatal letter — and that letter is the chief, the most overwhelming proof of the prisoner's having committed robbery! ‘I'll beg from everyone, and if I can't get it, I'll murder my father and take the envelope with the pink ribbon from under his mattress, as soon as Ivan has gone.’ A complete program for the murder, we're told — so it must have been him. ‘Everything happened exactly as he wrote it,’ cries the prosecutor.”

“But in the first place, it's the letter of a drunken man, written in a fit of temper; second, he writes about the envelope from what he'd heard from Smerdyakov, once again, since he'd never seen the envelope himself; and third, yes, he wrote it — but how can you prove that he actually did it? Did the prisoner take the envelope from under the pillow? Did he find the money? Did that money even exist? And was it for the money that the prisoner ran off, if you'll recall? He ran off in frantic haste not to steal, but to find out where she was — the woman who had destroyed him. He wasn't running to carry out some plan, to act on what he'd written — that is, not to commit a premeditated robbery — he ran suddenly, spontaneously, in a fit of jealous rage. Yes! I'll be told, but once he got there and murdered him, he grabbed the money too. But did he murder him at all? The charge of robbery I reject with indignation. A man can't be accused of robbery if it's impossible to state precisely what he stole — that's an axiom. But did he murder him without robbing him — did he murder him at all? Is that proven? Isn't that, too, a piece of fiction?”

title: XII. And There Was No Murder Either
paragraphs: “Allow me, gentlemen of the jury, to remind you that a man's life hangs in the balance, and that you must proceed carefully. We've heard the prosecutor himself admit that, until today, he hesitated to accuse the prisoner of the crime's full, conscious premeditation — he held back until he saw that fatal drunken letter, produced in court today. ‘Everything was done exactly as written.’ But I say again — he was running to her, to find her, purely in order to learn where she was. That's a fact beyond dispute. Had she been at home, he wouldn't have run off at all; he'd have stayed at her side, and so wouldn't have done what he'd promised in the letter. He ran off suddenly, by accident, and by that time he very likely didn't even remember his own drunken letter. ‘He snatched up the pestle,’ they say, and you'll recall how an entire edifice of psychology was constructed on that pestle — why he was bound to see it as a weapon, to snatch it up, and so on and so forth. A rather commonplace idea occurs to me here: what if that pestle hadn't been in plain sight, hadn't been lying on the shelf where the prisoner grabbed it, but had been put away in a cupboard instead? It wouldn't have caught his eye, and he'd have run off unarmed, empty-handed, and then he certainly wouldn't have killed anyone. So how can I possibly treat that pestle as proof of premeditation?”

“Yes, but he talked in the taverns about murdering his father, and two days before, on the evening he wrote his drunken letter, he was quiet and only quarreled with a shopkeeper — because, of course, a Karamazov simply can't help quarreling! But my answer to that is: if he'd really been planning such a murder in line with his letter, he certainly wouldn't have quarreled even with a shopkeeper, and probably wouldn't have gone into the tavern at all, because a man plotting such a crime seeks quiet, seeks seclusion, tries to make himself invisible, to avoid being seen or heard — and not out of calculation, but by instinct. Gentlemen of the jury, the psychological method cuts both ways, and we can wield it too. As for all that shouting in taverns over the course of the month, don't we often hear children, or drunks coming out of a tavern, shout, ‘I'll kill you’? And yet they don't murder anyone. And that fatal letter — isn't that simply drunken irritability too? Isn't it simply the shout of a brawler outside a tavern — ‘I'll kill you! I'll kill the lot of you!’? Why not? Why couldn't it be exactly that? What reason do we have to call that letter ‘fatal’ rather than merely absurd? Because his father was found murdered, because a witness saw the prisoner running out of the garden with a weapon in his hand and was knocked down by him — therefore, we're told, everything happened just as he'd planned in writing, and the letter wasn't ‘absurd’ but ‘fatal.’”

“Now, thank God, we've arrived at the real point: ‘since he was in the garden, he must have murdered him.’ In those few words — ‘since he was, then he must’ — lies the whole of the prosecution's case. He was there, so he must have done it. And what if there is no ‘must’ about it, even granting he was there? Oh, I admit the chain of evidence — the coincidences — really is suggestive. But examine each of these facts separately, apart from how they connect. Why, for instance, does the prosecution refuse to accept the truth of the prisoner's statement that he ran away from his father's window? Remember the sarcasm the prosecutor indulged in over the sudden, ‘pious’ feelings that came over the murderer. But what if there really was something of the kind — a feeling of religious awe, if not filial respect? ‘My mother must have been praying for me at that moment,’ were the prisoner's own words at the preliminary inquiry, and so he ran off the moment he'd convinced himself Madame Svyetlov wasn't in his father's house. ‘But he couldn't have convinced himself just by looking through the window,’ the prosecutor objects. But why couldn't he? Why not? The window opened at the signal the prisoner gave. Some word might have been spoken by Fyodor Pavlovitch, some exclamation, that showed the prisoner she wasn't there. Why should we assume everything happened exactly as we picture it, exactly as we've made up our minds to picture it? A thousand things can happen in real life that elude even the shrewdest imagination.”

“‘Yes, but Grigory saw the door open, so the prisoner must certainly have been inside the house, and therefore he killed him.’ Now, about that door, gentlemen of the jury.... Notice that we have only a single witness's statement about that door, and he was, at the time, in such a condition that— But suppose the door really was open; suppose the prisoner lied in denying it, out of an instinct for self-preservation, natural enough given his position; suppose he really did go into the house — well, what then? How does it follow that, because he was there, he committed the murder? He might have burst in, run through the rooms, might have shoved his father aside, might have struck him — but the moment he was sure Madame Svyetlov wasn't there, he may have run off rejoicing that she wasn't there and that he hadn't killed his father. And it may have been precisely because he'd escaped the temptation to kill his father, because his conscience was clear and he was rejoicing at not having killed him, that he was capable of a pure feeling — pity, compassion — and jumped down off the fence a minute later to help Grigory, whom he'd knocked down in his agitation.”

“With terrible eloquence the prosecutor has described for us the dreadful state of the prisoner's mind at Mokroe, when love once again lay open before him, calling him to a new life — while love was impossible for him, since he had his father's bloodstained corpse behind him, and, beyond that corpse, retribution. And yet the prosecutor allowed him this love, which he explained, following his own method, by talking about his drunkenness, about a criminal being led to execution, about the end still being far off, and so on and so forth. But again I ask, Mr. Prosecutor: haven't you invented an entirely new man here? Is the prisoner really so coarse, so heartless, that he could think, at such a moment, of love and of schemes to dodge punishment, if his hands had truly been stained with his father's blood? No, no, no! The moment it became clear to him that she loved him and was calling him to her side, promising him new happiness — oh, then, I insist, the impulse toward suicide must have doubled, tripled in him, and he must have killed himself, had his father's murder weighed on his conscience. Oh, no — he wouldn't have forgotten where his pistols were! I know the prisoner: the savage, stony heartlessness the prosecutor attributes to him doesn't square with his character. He would have killed himself — that's certain. He didn't kill himself only because ‘his mother's prayers had saved him,’ and because he was innocent of his father's blood. That night at Mokroe, all his trouble, all his grief, was over old Grigory alone — he was praying to God that the old man would recover, that the blow hadn't been fatal, that he wouldn't have to answer for it. Why not accept this reading of the facts? What reliable proof do we have that the prisoner is lying?”

“But at once we'll be told again: ‘There's his father's corpse! If he ran off without murdering him, then who did?’ Here again, I repeat, you have the whole of the prosecution's logic. Who murdered him, if not the prisoner? There's no one to put in his place.”

“Gentlemen of the jury, is that really so? Is it truly, positively true that there's no one else at all? We've heard the prosecutor count off, on his fingers, everyone who was in that house that night. There were five of them; three of them, I agree, couldn't possibly have been responsible — the murdered man himself, old Grigory, and his wife. That leaves the prisoner and Smerdyakov. And the prosecutor dramatically declares that the prisoner pointed to Smerdyakov simply because he had no one else to point to — that if there'd been a sixth person, even the mere shadow of a sixth person, he'd have abandoned the charge against Smerdyakov at once, out of shame, and accused that other person instead. But, gentlemen of the jury, why can't I draw the exact opposite conclusion? There are two people — the prisoner and Smerdyakov. Why can't I say that you accuse my client simply because you have no one else to accuse? And you have no one else to accuse only because you've already decided to rule Smerdyakov out of all suspicion.”

“True, Smerdyakov is accused only by the prisoner, his two brothers, and Madame Svyetlov. But there are others pointing to him as well: there are vague rumors, a question, a suspicion, a murky report, a certain feeling of anticipation. Finally we have a combination of facts that's quite suggestive, even if, I admit, inconclusive. First, there's the fit itself, occurring precisely on the day of the catastrophe, for whose genuineness the prosecutor has felt obliged, for some reason, to mount a careful defense. Then there's Smerdyakov's sudden suicide on the eve of the trial. Then there's the equally startling testimony given today in this court by the elder of the prisoner's brothers, who had believed in his brother's guilt but today produced a bundle of notes and declared Smerdyakov the murderer. Oh, I fully share the court's and the prosecutor's conviction that Ivan Karamazov is suffering from brain fever, that his statement may genuinely be a desperate, delirium-born attempt to save his brother by pinning the guilt on a dead man. But even so — Smerdyakov's name is spoken again, again there's a hint of mystery. Something remains unexplained, incomplete. And perhaps someday it will be explained. But let's not go into that now. More on that later.”

“The court has decided to press on with the trial, but in the meantime I might offer a few remarks on the character sketch of Smerdyakov the prosecutor drew with such subtlety and skill. Much as I admire his talent, I can't agree with him. I've visited Smerdyakov, I've seen him, I've talked with him, and he made a very different impression on me. His health was poor, that's true — but in character, in spirit, he was nothing like the weak man the prosecutor has made him out to be. I found no trace in him of the timidity the prosecutor made so much of. There was no simplicity about him either. What I found, on the contrary, was an extreme distrustfulness, hidden behind a mask of naïveté, and an intelligence of considerable reach. The prosecutor was too easily fooled in taking him for feeble-minded. He made a very definite impression on me: I came away convinced he was a distinctly spiteful creature, excessively ambitious, vindictive, and consumed with envy. I made some inquiries: he resented his parentage, was ashamed of it, and would clench his teeth remembering that he was the son of ‘stinking Lizaveta.’ He treated the servant Grigory and his wife, who had cared for him as a child, with disrespect. He cursed and sneered at Russia. He dreamed of going to France and becoming a Frenchman. He often said he lacked the means to do so. My impression is that he loved no one but himself, and had a strangely high opinion of himself. His idea of culture began and ended with good clothes, clean shirtfronts, and polished boots. Believing himself to be Fyodor Pavlovitch's illegitimate son (there's evidence for this), he may well have resented his position compared with that of his master's legitimate sons. They had everything, he had nothing. They had every right, they had the inheritance, while he had only the kitchen. He told me himself that he'd helped Fyodor Pavlovitch put the notes into the envelope. The fate of that sum — money that would have made his fortune — must have been galling to him. What's more, he saw three thousand roubles in fresh, rainbow-colored notes (I asked him about that on purpose). Oh, beware of showing an ambitious, envious man a large pile of money all at once! And that was the first time he'd ever seen so much money in one man's hands. The sight of those rainbow-colored notes may well have left a morbid impression on his imagination — though without any immediate consequence.”

“The talented prosecutor, with remarkable subtlety, laid out for us every argument for and against the theory of Smerdyakov's guilt, and asked, in particular, what motive he could have had for faking a fit. But he may not have been faking at all — the fit may have come on quite naturally, and just as naturally passed off, with the sick man recovering, not fully perhaps, but regaining enough consciousness, as often happens with epileptics.”

“The prosecutor asks at what moment Smerdyakov could have committed the murder. But it's quite easy to point to that moment. He might have woken from a deep sleep (since he'd only been asleep — an epileptic fit is always followed by deep sleep) at the very instant old Grigory shouted at the top of his lungs, ‘Parricide!’ That cry, in the dark stillness, might well have woken Smerdyakov, whose sleep may have been lighter just then — he might naturally have woken up an hour earlier than usual.”

“Getting out of bed, he goes, almost without knowing why, with no clear purpose, toward the sound, to see what's happening. His head is still clouded from the attack, his faculties half asleep — but once in the garden he walks toward the lit windows, and hears terrible news from his master, who would, of course, be glad to see him. His mind snaps into action at once. He hears every detail from his frightened master, and gradually, in his disordered brain, an idea takes shape — terrible, but seductive, irresistibly logical: kill the old man, take the three thousand, and pin the whole blame on his young master. A savage lust for money, for plunder, might well have seized him the moment he realized he was safe from detection. Oh, these sudden, irresistible impulses come so often when the opportunity presents itself — especially in murderers who had no prior intention of committing murder at all. And Smerdyakov may well have gone in and carried out his plan. With what weapon? Why, with any stone he picked up in the garden. But for what purpose, to what end? Why, for the three thousand roubles — which meant a whole new life for him. Oh, I'm not contradicting myself — the money may well have existed. And perhaps Smerdyakov alone knew where to find it, knew where his master kept it. And the wrapping of the money — that torn envelope on the floor?”

“A moment ago, as the prosecutor was laying out his subtle theory — that only an inexperienced thief like Karamazov would have left the envelope on the floor, and not someone like Smerdyakov, who'd have taken care not to leave evidence against himself — I thought, as I listened, that I was hearing something oddly familiar. And would you believe it — I heard that exact argument, that exact conjecture about how Karamazov would have behaved, precisely two days earlier, from Smerdyakov himself. What's more, it struck me at the time. I had the impression there was something artificial about his simplicity — that he was in a hurry to plant the idea in my mind so I'd take it for my own. He insinuated it, as it were. Didn't he insinuate that same idea at the inquiry, and suggest it to the talented prosecutor as well?”

“I'll be asked, ‘What about the old woman, Grigory's wife? She heard the sick man moaning close by, all night long.’ Yes, she heard it — but that testimony is extremely unreliable. I once knew a lady who complained bitterly of having been kept up all night by a dog barking in the yard. Yet the poor animal, it turned out, had only yelped once or twice all night. And that's only natural. If someone's asleep and hears a groan, they wake up, annoyed at being disturbed, and immediately fall back asleep. Two hours later, another groan — they wake, then fall back asleep again; and the same thing happens two hours after that — three times in all, over the whole night. The next morning, the sleeper wakes and complains that someone was groaning all night and kept them awake. And it's bound to feel that way to them: they don't remember the two-hour stretches of sleep in between — only the moments of waking — so they come away feeling they were kept up the entire night.”

“But why, why, the prosecutor asks, didn't Smerdyakov confess in his final letter? Why did his conscience prompt him to take one step, and not both? But, forgive me — conscience implies repentance, and the suicide may have felt not repentance at all, but only despair. Despair and repentance are two very different things. Despair can be vindictive and unforgiving, and a man taking his own life may well have felt only redoubled hatred for those he'd envied his whole life long.”

“Gentlemen of the jury, beware of a miscarriage of justice! What in everything I've just set before you is truly so unlikely? Find the flaw in my reasoning, find the impossibility, the absurdity in it. And if there is even a shadow of possibility, even a shadow of probability, in what I've proposed, do not convict him. And is it only a shadow? I swear by everything sacred — I fully believe in the account of the murder I've just given you. What troubles me, what outrages me, is that out of this whole mass of facts the prosecution has piled up against the prisoner, there isn't one single certain, irrefutable fact among them. And yet this unfortunate man is to be destroyed by the sheer accumulation of these facts. Yes, the cumulative effect is terrible: the blood, the blood dripping from his fingers, the bloodstained shirt, the dark night ringing with the cry ‘Parricide!’, and the old man falling with his skull broken. And then the mass of phrases, statements, gestures, shouts! Oh, all this carries such weight — it can bias the mind so easily. But, gentlemen of the jury — can it bias yours? Remember, you've been given absolute power to bind and to loose — but the greater the power, the more terrible the responsibility that comes with it.”

“I don't retreat one inch from what I've just said, but suppose, for a moment, that I agreed with the prosecution — that my unlucky client had indeed stained his hands with his father's blood. This is only a hypothesis, I repeat; I never doubt his innocence for one instant. But very well — let's say my client is guilty of parricide. Even then, hear me out. There's something more I need to say to you, because I sense there must be a great struggle underway in your hearts and minds.... Forgive me for speaking of your hearts and minds, gentlemen of the jury, but I want to be honest and sincere to the very end. Let all of us be sincere!”

At this point the speech was interrupted by rather loud applause. Those last words, indeed, were spoken with such a note of sincerity that everyone felt he truly might have something more to say, and that whatever he was about to say would matter a great deal. But the presiding judge, hearing the applause, warned loudly that he would clear the court if it happened again. Every sound died away, and Fetyukovitch began again, his voice now full of feeling, utterly unlike the tone he'd used so far.

title: XIII. A Corrupter Of Thought
paragraphs: “It's not just the accumulation of facts that threatens to destroy my client, gentlemen of the jury,” he began. “What's truly damning for my client is one single fact — the dead body of his father. Had this been an ordinary murder case, you would have rejected the charge, given how trivial, incomplete, and fantastical the evidence is when you examine each part of it separately — or, at the very least, you'd have hesitated to ruin a man's life purely out of the prejudice against him that he has, alas, all too thoroughly earned. But this isn't an ordinary murder case — it's a case of parricide. That fact weighs on people's minds, and weighs so heavily that even the triviality and incompleteness of the evidence starts to feel less trivial, less incomplete, even to an unbiased mind. How can such a prisoner possibly be acquitted? What if he really did commit the murder, and walks free unpunished? That's what nearly everyone feels in their heart, almost without meaning to, purely on instinct.”

“Yes, it's a terrible thing to shed a father's blood — the father who fathered me, who loved me, who never spared himself for my sake, who worried over my childhood illnesses, who spent his whole life anxious for my happiness, who lived through my joys and my successes. To murder such a father — that's unthinkable. Gentlemen of the jury, what is a father — a real father? What does that great word actually mean? What idea lies behind that name? We've already sketched, in part, what a true father is, and what he ought to be. In the case now occupying us so completely, the one weighing so heavily on our hearts — in this case, the father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, did not match that idea of a father we've just described. That's the misfortune of it. And indeed, some fathers are exactly that — a misfortune. Let's look a little more closely at this misfortune: we mustn't flinch from anything, gentlemen of the jury, given the gravity of the decision before you. It's precisely our duty not to shy away from any idea, like children, or like frightened women, as the talented prosecutor so aptly put it.”

“But in the course of his impassioned speech, my esteemed opponent (and he was my opponent before I ever opened my mouth) exclaimed more than once, ‘Oh, I won't leave the prisoner's defense entirely to the lawyer who's come down from Petersburg. I accuse, but I defend too!’ He said this several times — but he forgot to mention that if this terrible prisoner was grateful, for twenty-three years, for a single pound of nuts given him by the only man who'd ever shown him kindness as a child in his father's house, might not such a man just as easily have remembered, for twenty-three years, how he once ran around his father's back yard ‘without boots on his feet, his little trousers hanging by one button’ — to borrow the kindhearted Doctor Herzenstube's own phrase?”

“Oh, gentlemen of the jury, why do we need to look any closer at this misfortune, why repeat what we all already know? What did my client find when he arrived here, at his father's house, and why paint my client as a heartless egotist, a monster? He is uncontrolled, he is wild and unruly — we're trying him for that right now — but who is responsible for the life he's led? Who is responsible for the disgraceful upbringing he received, despite his excellent nature and his grateful, sensitive heart? Did anyone teach him to think clearly? Did anyone give him an education? Did a single soul love him, even a little, in his childhood? My client was left to the mercy of Providence like an animal in the field. Perhaps he longed, after years of separation, to see his father again. A thousand times, perhaps, recalling his childhood, he may have driven off the loathsome phantoms that haunted his childish dreams, and longed with his whole heart to embrace his father and forgive him! And what awaited him instead? Cynical mockery, suspicion, squabbling over money. He heard nothing but vile talk and depraved advice, poured out daily over the brandy bottle, and at last he watched his own father steal his mistress from him, using his own money to do it. Oh, gentlemen of the jury, that was cruel, and it was vile! And that old man was forever complaining about his son's disrespect and cruelty. He slandered him in society, wronged him, defamed him, bought up his unpaid debts to get him thrown in prison.”

“Gentlemen of the jury, people like my client — fierce, unruly, uncontrolled on the surface — are sometimes, most often in fact, remarkably tender-hearted underneath, only they don't show it. Don't laugh — don't laugh at what I'm saying! The talented prosecutor laughed without mercy, a moment ago, at my client for loving Schiller — for loving the sublime and the beautiful! I wouldn't have laughed at that, in his place. Yes, such natures — oh, let me speak up for natures like this, so often, so cruelly misunderstood — such natures often thirst for tenderness, for goodness, for justice, precisely as a counterweight to themselves, to their own unruliness, their own ferocity — they thirst for it unconsciously. Passionate, fierce on the outside, they're painfully capable of loving a woman, for instance, with a spiritual, elevated love. Again, don't laugh at me — this is very often true of natures like this. But they can't hide their passions — sometimes very coarse ones — and that's what's conspicuous, that's what gets noticed, while the inner man goes unseen. Their passions burn out quickly; but beside some noble, elevated soul, that seemingly coarse, rough man will search for a new life, will try to correct himself, to become better, to grow noble and honorable, ‘sublime and beautiful’ — however much that phrase has been mocked.”

“I said just now that I wouldn't venture to touch on my client's engagement. But let me say half a word about it. What we heard a moment ago wasn't testimony — it was only the outburst of a frenzied, vengeful woman, and it wasn't for her — oh, not for her! — to accuse him of betrayal, when it was she who betrayed him! Had she had even a little time to reflect, she wouldn't have given testimony like that. Oh, don't believe her! No — my client is not the monster she called him!”

“The Lover of Mankind, on the eve of His Crucifixion, said: ‘I am the Good Shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, so that not one of them may be lost.’ Let us not be the reason a man's soul is lost!”

“A moment ago I asked what ‘father’ means, and declared that it's a great word, a precious name. But we must use words honestly, gentlemen, and I'll venture to call things by their right names: a father like old Karamazov cannot be called a father, and doesn't deserve to be. Filial love for an unworthy father is an absurdity, an impossibility. Love cannot be conjured out of nothing — only God can create something from nothing.”

“‘Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath,’ the apostle writes, from a heart burning with love. I don't quote these sacred words for my client's sake — I mention them for the sake of all fathers. Who's authorized me to preach to fathers? No one. But as a man, as a citizen, I make my appeal — vivos voco! Our time on earth is short; we do a great many wicked things, we say a great many wicked words. So let's all seize this favorable moment, now that we're gathered together, to say one good word to one another. That's what I'm doing: while I'm standing here, I'll make the most of the chance. This tribune wasn't given to us by the highest authority for nothing — all of Russia is listening! I'm not speaking only to the fathers present here; I cry out to every father: ‘Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath.’ Yes — let us first fulfill Christ's commandment ourselves, and only then dare to expect it of our children. Otherwise we're not fathers at all, but enemies of our children — and they're not our children, but our enemies, and we've made them our enemies with our own hands. ‘Whatever measure you use, it will be measured back to you’ — that's not my saying, that's the Gospel precept: measure others as they measure you. How can we blame children if they measure us by our own measure?”

“Not long ago, a servant girl in Finland was suspected of having secretly given birth to a child. She was watched, and a box no one had known anything about was found tucked in a corner of the loft, behind some bricks. It was opened, and inside lay the body of a newborn infant, whom she had killed. In the same box were found the skeletons of two other babies, which, by her own confession, she had killed the moment they were born.”

“Gentlemen of the jury, was that woman a mother to her children? She gave birth to them, certainly — but was she a mother to them? Would anyone dare give her that sacred name, mother? Let's be bold, gentlemen — let's be daring, even. It's our duty to be so at this moment, and not to shy away from certain words and ideas, like the Moscow merchants' wives in Ostrovsky's play, who are frightened by the mere sound of certain words. No — let us prove that the progress of recent years has touched even us, and let us state plainly: a father isn't merely the man who fathers a child — he's the man who fathers it and then does his duty by it.”

“Oh, of course, there's the other meaning, the other interpretation of the word ‘father,’ which insists that any father — even a monster, even one who's the enemy of his own children — still remains my father, purely and simply because he begot me. But this is, so to speak, a mystical meaning, one I can't grasp with my intellect, but can only accept by faith — or better, on faith — like many other things I don't understand but which religion instructs me to believe. But in that case, let it stay outside the sphere of ordinary life. In the sphere of ordinary life — which does have its own rights, but which also lays great duties and obligations upon us — in that sphere, if we want to act humanely, in a Christian way, in fact, we must, we ought to, act only on convictions justified by reason and experience, convictions that have passed through the crucible of analysis. In a word, we must act rationally, not as though in a dream or a delirium, so that we don't harm anyone, so that we don't mistreat and destroy a man. Only then will it be real Christian work — not merely mystical, but rational and humane....”

There was a burst of applause at this point from many parts of the courtroom, but Fetyukovitch waved his hands, as though begging them to let him finish without interruption. The court fell silent at once. The speaker went on.

“Do you suppose, gentlemen, that our children, as they grow up and begin to reason, can avoid questions like these? No, they cannot — and we won't be able to hold them to some impossible restraint. The sight of an unworthy father inevitably raises tormenting questions in a young mind, especially when he compares that father with the excellent fathers of his companions. The conventional answer to such a question runs: ‘He begot you, you are his flesh and blood, and therefore you're bound to love him.’ And the young person, almost against his will, reflects: ‘But did he love me when he begot me?’ he wonders, more and more puzzled. ‘Was it for my sake that he begot me? He didn't know me — didn't even know my sex — at that moment, at the moment of passion, perhaps inflamed by wine, and all he's passed on to me is a taste for drink — that's all he's ever done for me.... Why am I bound to love him simply for begetting me, when he's cared nothing for me all my life since?’”

“Oh, perhaps those questions strike you as coarse and cruel, but you can't expect an impossible restraint from a young mind. ‘Drive nature out the door and it'll fly back in through the window’ — and above all, let's not be afraid of words, but settle the question according to the dictates of reason and humanity, not mystical ideas. How should it be settled? Like this: let the son stand before his father and ask him, ‘Father, tell me — why must I love you? Father, show me why I must love you’ — and if that father can answer him, can give him good reason, then we have a real, normal, parental bond, resting not on mystical prejudice but on a rational, responsible, and strictly humane foundation. But if he can't, then the family tie ends there. He is no father to the son, and the son has every right to look on him as a stranger, even an enemy. Our tribune here, gentlemen of the jury, ought to be a school for sound and honest ideas.”

(Here the speaker was interrupted by uncontrollable, almost frantic applause. It wasn't the whole audience, of course, but a good half of it applauded. The fathers and mothers in the room applauded. Shrieks and cries rose from the gallery, where the ladies sat. Handkerchiefs were waved. The presiding judge rang his bell as hard as he could. He was clearly irritated by the audience's behavior, but didn't dare clear the court as he'd threatened to. Even distinguished figures — elderly men with medals on their chests, seated in the reserved seats behind the judges — applauded the speaker and waved their handkerchiefs. So that once the noise died down, the judge simply repeated his stern threat to clear the court, and Fetyukovitch, excited and triumphant, continued his speech.)

“Gentlemen of the jury, you remember that terrible night we've heard so much about today, when the son climbed the fence and stood face to face with the very man who had fathered him — his enemy, his tormentor. I insist most emphatically that it wasn't for money that he ran to his father's house: the charge of robbery is absurd, as I've already shown. And it wasn't to murder him that he broke into the house — oh, no! Had that been his plan, he'd at the very least have taken the precaution of arming himself beforehand. He snatched up the brass pestle on instinct, without even knowing why. Granted that he tricked his father by tapping at the window, granted that he made his way inside — I've said already that I don't believe that story for a moment, but let's suppose it, just for argument's sake. Gentlemen, I swear to you by everything sacred: had it been anyone but his father — an ordinary enemy — he would, after running through the rooms and confirming the woman wasn't there, have made off at once, without laying a hand on his rival. He might have struck him, shoved him aside perhaps — nothing more — because he had neither the thought nor the time to spare for that. All he wanted was to know where she was. But his father — his own father! The mere sight of the father who had hated him since childhood, who had been his enemy, his tormentor, and was now his unnatural rival — that alone was enough! A wave of hatred swept over him, involuntary, irresistible, clouding his reason entirely. It all rose up in a single instant! It was a fit of madness, of insanity — but also, at the same time, an impulse of nature, irresistibly and unconsciously — as everything in nature does — avenging the violation of its own eternal laws.”

“But even then, the prisoner did not murder him — I insist on that, I proclaim it! No — he only brandished the pestle in a burst of furious disgust, with no intention of killing him, with no idea that he would kill him. Had he not had that fatal pestle in his hand, he'd have done no more than knock his father down, perhaps — but he wouldn't have killed him. As he ran off, he had no idea whether he'd killed the old man or not. A killing like that isn't murder. A killing like that isn't parricide. No — such a killing can't be called parricide at all. Only prejudice could reckon such a killing as parricide.”

“But I appeal to you again, and again, from the very depths of my soul: did this murder actually happen? Gentlemen of the jury, if we convict him, if we punish him, he'll say to himself: ‘These people never did anything for my upbringing, for my education, nothing to improve my lot, nothing to make me a better man. These people never fed me, never gave me drink, never visited me in prison or in my nakedness — and now they've sent me off to hard labor. I owe them nothing now, I owe no one anything, ever again. They are wicked, and I will be wicked. They are cruel, and I will be cruel.’ That's what he'll say, gentlemen of the jury. And I swear to you — by finding him guilty, all you'll do is make things easier for him: you'll ease his conscience, he'll curse the blood he shed and feel no regret for it. And at the same time you'll destroy in him any chance of becoming a new man, because he'll remain, for the rest of his life, exactly as wicked and blind as he is now.”

“But do you want to punish him — fearfully, terribly, with the most awful punishment imaginable — and at the same time save him, bring his soul back to life? If so, overwhelm him with mercy! You'll see, you'll hear, how he trembles, how he's struck with awe. ‘How can I bear this mercy? How can I bear so much love? Am I worthy of it?’ — that's what he'll cry out.”

“Oh, I know, I know that heart, that wild but grateful heart, gentlemen of the jury! It will bow before your mercy; it thirsts for some great, loving act, and it will melt, it will rise upward. There are souls which, in their narrowness, blame the whole world for their troubles. But subdue a soul like that with mercy, show it love, and it will curse its own past, because there is so much good still in it. Such a heart will open, and see that God is merciful, that men are good and just. He'll be struck with awe, crushed by remorse, by the vast weight of obligation now laid on him. And he won't say then, ‘I owe them nothing’ — he'll say, ‘I am guilty before every man, more unworthy than all of them.’ With tears of repentance, with sharp, tender anguish, he'll cry out: ‘Others are better than I am — they wanted to save me, not destroy me!’ Oh, this act of mercy is so easy for you to grant — because, given the utter absence of anything resembling real proof, it will be far too terrible for you to pronounce the words: ‘Yes, he is guilty.’”

“Better to acquit ten guilty men than to punish one innocent one! Do you hear that — do you hear that majestic voice, echoing down from the glorious history of the century before ours? It's hardly my place, an insignificant man like me, to remind you that the Russian court exists not only to punish, but also to save the criminal! Let other nations think in terms of retribution and the letter of the law; we will hold fast to the spirit, to the meaning behind it — the salvation and the reform of the lost. If that's true, if that's what Russia and her justice really are, then she may move forward with a clear conscience! Don't try to frighten us with your frenzied troikas, the ones every other nation recoils from in disgust. Not some runaway troika, but the stately chariot of Russia will move forward calmly, majestically, toward its goal. In your hands lies my client's fate; in your hands lies the fate of Russian justice. Defend it. Save it. Prove that there are men watching over it, that it rests in good hands!”

title: XIV. The Peasants Stand Firm
paragraphs: That was how Fetyukovitch ended his speech, and the audience's enthusiasm broke out like an unstoppable storm. There was no question of holding it back: the women wept, many of the men wept too, even two eminent figures shed tears. The presiding judge gave way, and even put off ringing his bell. To suppress such enthusiasm would have been to suppress something sacred, as the ladies cried afterward. The speaker himself was genuinely moved.

And it was at this very moment that Ippolit Kirillovitch rose to raise certain objections. People looked at him with something like hatred. “What? What does this mean? He actually dares to object,” the ladies muttered. But if every woman in the room, including his own wife, had protested, nothing could have stopped him at that moment. He was pale, shaking with emotion; his first sentences were barely intelligible — he gasped for breath, could hardly get the words out clearly, lost his train of thought. But he soon pulled himself together. Of this second speech of his I'll quote only a few sentences.

“... I'm accused of having spun a romance. But what is this defense, if not one romance piled on top of another? All that was missing was the verse. Fyodor Pavlovitch, while waiting for his mistress, tears open the envelope and throws it on the floor — and we're even told what he supposedly said while doing this strange thing. Isn't that a flight of fancy? And what proof do we have that he actually took the money out? Who heard him say it? The feeble-minded Smerdyakov, transformed into a Byronic hero avenging society for his illegitimate birth — isn't that a romance straight out of Byron? And the son who breaks into his father's house and murders him without murdering him isn't even a romance — it's a sphinx posing a riddle it can't solve itself. If he murdered him, he murdered him — what on earth is the meaning of murdering him without having murdered him? Who can make any sense of that?”

“Then we're told that our tribune is a tribune of true and sound ideas, and from that tribune of ‘sound ideas’ comes a solemn declaration that calling the murder of a father ‘parricide’ is nothing but a prejudice! But if parricide is a prejudice, and every child is entitled to ask his father why he should love him, what becomes of us? What becomes of the foundations of society? What becomes of the family? Parricide, it seems, is nothing but a bogeyman invented to frighten Moscow merchants' wives. The most precious, most sacred guarantees for the destiny and future of Russian justice are being presented to us in a twisted, frivolous form, for one purpose only — to justify what cannot be justified. ‘Oh, crush him with mercy,’ cries the counsel for the defense — but that's exactly what the criminal wants, and tomorrow we'll see just how crushed he is. And isn't the counsel for the defense being too modest, asking only for an acquittal? Why not endow a charity in the parricide's honor, to commemorate his feat for future generations? Religion and the Gospel are being corrected for us — all mysticism, we're told, and ours is the only true Christianity, one that's been run through the sieve of reason and common sense. And so they set before us a false imitation of Christ! ‘Whatever measure you use will be measured back to you,’ cried the counsel for the defense, drawing the instant conclusion that Christ is teaching us to measure others exactly as they measure us — and this, from the tribune of truth and sound sense! We only dip into the Gospel on the eve of making a speech, so as to dazzle the audience with our familiarity with what is, after all, a rather remarkable text, one that can be put to good effect — anything to serve the purpose! But what Christ actually commands is something entirely different: He warns us against exactly this, because that's how the wicked world behaves, and instead tells us to forgive, to turn the other cheek, and not to measure our persecutors by their own measure. That is what our God has taught us — not that forbidding children to murder their fathers is some prejudice. And we will not, from the tribune of truth and sound sense, go about correcting the Gospel of our Lord, whom the counsel for the defense condescends to call merely ‘the crucified lover of mankind,’ in defiance of all Orthodox Russia, which cries out to Him, ‘For Thou art our God!’”

At this point the presiding judge stepped in and reined in the overzealous speaker, urging him not to exaggerate, not to overstep the bounds, and so on, as presiding judges always do in such situations. The audience, too, grew restless; there were even cries of indignation. Fetyukovitch didn't even bother to respond directly; he simply mounted the tribune, laid a hand on his heart, and, in a wounded voice, spoke a few words full of dignity. He touched again, lightly and ironically, on ‘romancing’ and ‘psychology,’ and at the right moment quoted, ‘Jupiter, you are angry, therefore you are wrong,’ which drew a burst of approving laughter from the audience, since Ippolit Kirillovitch bore no resemblance whatsoever to Jupiter. Then, on the subject of being accused of teaching the younger generation to murder their fathers, Fetyukovitch remarked, with great dignity, that he wouldn't even respond to that. As for the prosecutor's charge that he'd voiced unorthodox opinions, Fetyukovitch hinted that this was a personal insinuation, and that he'd expected, in this court, to be safe from accusations ‘damaging to my reputation as a citizen and a loyal subject.’ But the presiding judge cut him off here too, and Fetyukovitch closed his speech with a bow, amid a murmur of approval throughout the court. And in the opinion of our ladies, Ippolit Kirillovitch had been ‘crushed for good.’

Then the prisoner was given leave to speak. Mitya stood up, but said very little. He was terribly worn out, in body and mind alike. The look of strength and independence he'd worn that morning had almost entirely vanished. He seemed to have lived through something that day that had taught him, for the rest of his life, something important he'd never understood before. His voice was weak; he no longer shouted as he once had. There was a new note in his words — humility, defeat, submission.

“What am I to say, gentlemen of the jury? My hour of judgment has come — I feel the hand of God upon me! This is the end for an erring man! But before God, I say it again: I am innocent of my father's blood! For the last time, I say it: it wasn't I who killed him! I went astray, but I loved what is good. Every moment I strove to reform myself, and yet I lived like a wild animal. I thank the prosecutor — he told me a great deal about myself that I didn't know. But it isn't true that I killed my father — the prosecutor is mistaken there. I thank my counsel too. I wept, listening to him. But it isn't true that I killed my father, and he needn't have assumed it. And don't believe the doctors — I'm perfectly sane, only my heart is heavy. If you spare me, if you let me go, I'll pray for you. I'll become a better man. I give you my word before God that I will! And if you condemn me, I'll break my sword over my own head and kiss the pieces. But spare me — don't rob me of my God! I know myself — I'll rebel! My heart is heavy, gentlemen.... spare me!”

He nearly collapsed back into his seat; his voice broke; he could barely get out that last phrase. Then the judges moved on to putting their questions, and asked both sides to formulate their final positions.

But I won't go into the details. At last the jury rose to retire and confer. The presiding judge was exhausted, and so his closing charge to the jury was fairly weak. “Be impartial. Don't let yourselves be swayed by the eloquence of the defense — but weigh the arguments carefully all the same. Remember the heavy responsibility resting on you,” and so on, and so forth.

The jury withdrew, and the court adjourned. People got up, moved around, traded their pent-up impressions, refreshed themselves at the buffet. It was very late, nearly one in the morning, but nobody left — the tension was too great for anyone to think of rest. Everyone waited with a sinking heart — though perhaps that's putting it too strongly, since the ladies were merely in a state of hysterical impatience, their hearts untroubled. An acquittal, they were sure, was inevitable. They were all bracing themselves for a dramatic burst of general rejoicing. I have to admit there were plenty of men, too, who were convinced an acquittal was a certainty. Some were pleased, some frowned, and some were simply gloomy, not wanting to see him acquitted at all. Fetyukovitch himself was confident of success. He was surrounded by people congratulating him, fawning over him.

“There are,” he said to one group, as I was told afterward, “invisible threads that bind the counsel for the defense to the jury. You can feel them forming while you speak. I felt them. They're real. Our case is won. Set your minds at rest.”
“What will our peasants say now?” said one stout, sour-faced, pockmarked gentleman, a landowner from the neighborhood, walking up to a knot of men deep in conversation.
“But they're not all peasants. There are four government clerks among them.”
“Yes, there are clerks,” said a member of the district council, joining the group.
“And did you know that Nazaryev, the merchant with the medal, is on the jury?”
“What of it?”
“He's a man with a head on his shoulders.”
“But he never says a word.”

“He's not much of a talker, but so much the better for it. He doesn't need any lessons from the Petersburg man — he could teach all of Petersburg himself. He's the father of twelve children. Think of that!”
“Surely you don't imagine they won't acquit him?” one of our young officials exclaimed in another group.
“They'll acquit him for certain,” said a confident voice.

“It would be shameful, disgraceful, not to acquit him!” cried the official. “Suppose he really did kill him — there are fathers, and then there are fathers! And besides, he was in such a frenzy.... He may honestly have done nothing but swing that pestle through the air and knock the old man down by accident. But it was a shame they dragged the valet into it — that was simply an absurd theory. If I'd been in Fetyukovitch's place, I'd have just said flatly: ‘He murdered him — but he's not guilty, damn it all!’”
“That's more or less what he did say, only without the ‘damn it all!’”
“No, Mihail Semyonovitch, he all but said that too,” put in a third voice.
“Why, gentlemen, during Lent an actress was acquitted right here in our own town, after cutting the throat of her lover's lawful wife.”
“Oh, but she never finished cutting it.”
“Makes no difference. She started cutting it.”
“What did you make of what he said about children? Splendid, wasn't it?”
“Splendid!”
“And about mysticism too!”
“Oh, forget mysticism, do!” cried someone else. “Think of poor Ippolit and what's coming to him from this day forward. His wife will scratch his eyes out tomorrow over Mitya's acquittal.”
“Is she here?”
“What an idea! If she'd been here she'd have scratched them out right in the courtroom. She's home with a toothache. Heh heh heh!”
“Heh heh heh!”
In a third group:
“I dare say they'll acquit Mitenka after all.”
“I wouldn't be surprised if he turns the ‘Metropolis’ upside down tomorrow. He'll be drinking for ten days straight!”
“Oh, the devil!”
“The devil's bound to have a hand in it somewhere. Where else would he be, if not here?”
“Well, gentlemen, I'll grant it was eloquent. But all the same, it's not the done thing, cracking your father's skull with a pestle! What are we coming to?”
“The chariot! Do you remember that bit about the chariot?”
“Yes — he turned a cart into a chariot!”
“And tomorrow he'll turn the chariot back into a cart, whatever suits him at the time.”
“What crafty fellows there are these days! Is there any justice left in Russia at all?”

But the bell rang. The jury deliberated for exactly one hour — no more, no less. A deep silence fell over the court the moment the audience had taken their seats. I remember how the jurymen filed in. At last! I won't repeat the questions in order — in fact, I've forgotten them. I remember only the answer to the presiding judge's first and most important question: ‘Did the prisoner commit the murder for the sake of robbery, and with premeditation?’ (I don't recall the exact wording.) There was total silence. The jury foreman, the youngest of the clerks, pronounced, in a clear, loud voice, into the deathly stillness of the court:
“Yes, guilty!”

And the same answer followed every question: ‘Yes, guilty!’ — without a single word of mitigation. No one had expected this; nearly everyone had counted on at least a recommendation for mercy.
