The deathly silence in the court held for a moment — everyone seemed turned to stone, those who'd wanted a conviction no less than those who'd hoped for an acquittal. But that lasted only an instant, and then came a terrible uproar. Many of the men in the audience were pleased; some rubbed their hands together, not even trying to hide their satisfaction. Those who disagreed with the verdict looked crushed, shrugged, whispered to one another, but still seemed unable to take it in. But how can I describe the state the ladies were in? I thought there would be a riot. At first they could hardly believe their ears. Then, all at once, the whole courtroom rang with cries: ‘What does this mean? What next?’ They leapt to their feet. They seemed to imagine the verdict might still be reconsidered, reversed on the spot. At that instant Mitya suddenly stood up and cried out, in a heartbreaking voice, stretching his hands out before him:
“I swear by God and the dreadful Day of Judgment, I am not guilty of my father's blood! Katya, I forgive you! Brothers, friends — have pity on the other woman!”

He couldn't go on; he broke into a terrible sobbing wail that carried through the whole courtroom, in a strange, unnatural voice, unlike his own. From the farthest corner of the back gallery came a piercing shriek — it was Grushenka. She'd managed to talk her way back into the courtroom before the lawyers' closing speeches began. Mitya was led away. The sentencing was put off until the next day. The whole courtroom dissolved into an uproar, but I didn't stay to hear it. I remember only a few remarks I caught on the steps as I went out.
“He'll get twenty years in the mines!”
“Not a day less.”
“Well — our peasants held firm.”
“And finished off our Mitya.”

title: I. Plans For Mitya’s Escape
paragraphs: Very early, at nine in the morning, five days after the trial, Alyosha went to see Katerina Ivanovna, to discuss a matter that mattered a great deal to both of them, and to deliver a message. She received him and talked with him in the very room where she had once received Grushenka. In the next room, Ivan Fyodorovitch lay unconscious with a high fever. Right after the scene at the trial, Katerina Ivanovna had ordered the sick, unconscious man carried to her house, ignoring the inevitable gossip and the public's general disapproval. One of the two relatives living with her had left for Moscow immediately after the courtroom scene; the other had stayed. But even if both had gone, Katerina Ivanovna would have held to her resolve and gone on nursing the sick man, sitting by him day and night. Varvinsky and Herzenstube were attending him. The famous doctor had returned to Moscow, refusing to venture an opinion on how the illness would likely end. Though the doctors tried to encourage Katerina Ivanovna and Alyosha, it was clear they couldn't yet offer any real hope of recovery.

Alyosha came to see his sick brother twice a day. But this time he had particularly urgent business, and he could already tell how hard it would be to bring up the subject, and yet he was in a great hurry. He had another appointment that morning he couldn't put off, and there was no time to waste.

They had been talking for a quarter of an hour. Katerina Ivanovna was pale, utterly exhausted, and yet at the same time in a state of hysterical agitation. She had a feeling she already knew why Alyosha had come.

“Don't worry about his decision,” she told Alyosha, with confident emphasis. “One way or another, he's bound to come around to it. He has to escape. That unhappy man, that hero of honor and principle — not him, not Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but the man lying on the other side of that door, who has sacrificed himself for his brother” — Katya added, her eyes flashing — “told me the whole escape plan long ago. You know he's already opened negotiations.... I've told you some of it already.... You see, it will probably happen at the third stopping point from here, when the group of prisoners is being marched off to Siberia. Oh, that's a long way off yet. Ivan Fyodorovitch has already visited the superintendent at the third stop. But we still don't know who'll be in charge of the party, and there's no way to find that out so far in advance. Tomorrow, perhaps, I'll show you the whole plan in detail, the one Ivan Fyodorovitch left with me on the eve of the trial, in case it's needed.... That was when — do you remember? — you found us quarreling. He'd just gone downstairs, but when he saw you I made him come back — do you remember? Do you know what we were quarreling about then?”
“No, I don't,” said Alyosha.

“Of course he didn't tell you. It was about that escape plan. He'd told me the main idea three days before, and we started quarreling about it right away, and kept it up for three days. We quarreled because, when he told me that if Dmitri Fyodorovitch were convicted he'd escape abroad with that creature, I flew into a fury on the spot — I can't tell you why, I don't even know myself why.... Oh, of course, I was furious about that creature — furious that she, too, would go abroad with Dmitri!” Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed suddenly, her lips trembling with anger. “The moment Ivan Fyodorovitch saw how furious I was about that woman, he instantly assumed I was jealous of Dmitri, that I still loved him. That's how our first quarrel started. I wouldn't explain myself, I couldn't bring myself to ask forgiveness. I couldn't bear the thought that a man like that could suspect me of still loving that... when I myself had told him, long before, that I didn't love Dmitri, that I loved no one but him! It was purely my resentment at that creature that made me angry with him. Three days later, the evening you came, he brought me a sealed envelope, which I was to open at once if anything happened to him. Oh — he already foresaw his illness! He told me the envelope held the details of the escape, and that if he died, or fell dangerously ill, I was to save Mitya on my own. Then he left me money — nearly ten thousand — the very notes the prosecutor mentioned in his speech, having learned from someone that he'd sent them to be cashed. I was tremendously moved to find that Ivan Fyodorovitch hadn't given up on the idea of saving his brother, and was confiding this escape plan to me, even while he was still jealous of me, still convinced I loved Mitya. Oh, that was a sacrifice! No — you can't understand the greatness of such self-sacrifice, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I wanted to fall at his feet in reverence, but it occurred to me at once that he'd take it for nothing more than my joy at the thought of Mitya being saved — and he certainly would have thought exactly that! — and I was so outraged at the mere possibility of such an unjust thought on his part that I lost my temper all over again, and instead of kissing his feet, flew into a rage instead! Oh, I'm a wretched creature! It's my character, my terrible, wretched character! Oh, you'll see — I'll end up driving him away too, toward some other woman he can get along with better, the way it happened with Dmitri. But... no, I couldn't bear that, I'd kill myself. And when you came in that day, and I called out to you and told him to come back, I was so enraged by the look of contempt and hatred he turned on me that — do you remember? — I cried out to you that it was he, he alone, who'd convinced me his brother Dmitri was a murderer! I said that spiteful thing on purpose, to wound him again. He had never, never convinced me his brother was a murderer. On the contrary — it was I who convinced him! Oh, my vile temper was the cause of everything! I paved the way for that hideous scene at the trial. He wanted to show me he was an honorable man, that even if I loved his brother, he wouldn't destroy him out of revenge or jealousy. So he came to the court.... I'm the cause of it all — I alone am to blame!”

Katya had never made confessions like this to Alyosha before, and he sensed she'd reached that point of unbearable suffering where even the proudest heart is forced to crush its own pride and give way to grief. Oh, Alyosha knew of another terrible source of her present misery, though she'd carefully hidden it from him in the days since the trial — but it would somehow have been too painful for him if she'd sunk so low as to speak to him about it now. She was suffering over her ‘betrayal’ at the trial, and Alyosha sensed her conscience was pushing her to confess it to him — to him, Alyosha — with tears, with cries, writhing on the floor in hysterics. But he dreaded that moment and wanted, above all, to spare her. It made the errand he'd come on all the harder. He turned the conversation back to Mitya.

“It's all right, it's all right, don't worry about him!” she began again, sharply, stubbornly. “All that is only temporary — I know him, I know his heart better than anyone. You can be sure he'll agree to escape. It won't happen right away — he'll have time to make up his mind to it. By then Ivan Fyodorovitch will be well and will manage the whole thing himself, so I won't have to do anything with it. Don't worry — he'll agree to run. He's already agreed, in fact — do you suppose he'd give up that creature? And they won't let her go to him there, so he's bound to escape. It's you he's most afraid of — he's afraid you won't approve of his escaping, on moral grounds. But you must be generous enough to allow it, if your blessing matters so much to him,” Katya added, with a touch of spite. She paused, and smiled.

“He talks about some hymn,” she went on, “some cross he has to bear, some duty — I remember Ivan Fyodorovitch told me a great deal about it, and if you only knew how he talked!” Katya cried suddenly, unable to hold back her feeling. “If you knew how he loved that wretched man, right there while he was telling me — and how he hated him too, in that same moment, perhaps! And I listened to his story, to his tears, with sneering contempt. Brute — yes, I'm a brute. I'm the cause of his fever. But that man in prison isn't even capable of suffering,” Katya concluded irritably. “Can a man like that really suffer? Men like him never suffer!”

There was a note of hatred and contemptuous revulsion in her words. And yet it was she who had betrayed him. ‘Maybe it's because she senses how she's wronged him that she hates him, at moments like this,’ Alyosha thought to himself. He hoped it really was only ‘at moments.’ He caught a challenging note in Katya's last words, but he didn't rise to it.

“I sent for you this morning to get your promise that you'll persuade him yourself. Or do you also think escaping would be dishonorable, cowardly, or something... unchristian, perhaps?” Katya added, even more defiantly.

“Oh, no. I'll tell him everything,” Alyosha muttered. “He's asking you to come and see him today,” he blurted out suddenly, looking her straight in the face. She started, and drew back a little from him on the sofa.
“Me? Is that really possible?” she faltered, going pale.

“It's possible, and it ought to happen!” Alyosha began, growing more animated, speaking with emphasis. “He needs you especially right now. I wouldn't have raised the subject and troubled you if it weren't necessary. He's ill, he's beside himself, he keeps asking for you. He doesn't want to be reconciled with you — he only wants you to come and show yourself in his doorway. So much has happened to him since that day. He understands now that he's wronged you beyond all measure. He isn't asking your forgiveness — ‘It's impossible to forgive me,’ he says himself — only that you show yourself in his doorway.”
“It's all so sudden....” Katya faltered. “I've had a feeling, these past few days, that you'd come with exactly this message. I knew he'd ask me to come. It's impossible!”

“Let it be impossible — do it anyway. Just think: he's realized, for the first time in his life, how deeply he's wounded you; he never fully understood it before. He said, ‘If she refuses to come, I'll be unhappy my whole life.’ Do you hear that? Even though he's been sentenced to twenty years of hard labor, he's still making plans to be happy — isn't that pitiful? Think — you must visit him. Even though he's ruined, he's innocent,” broke from Alyosha like a challenge. “His hands are clean — there's no blood on them! For the sake of everything he's still going to suffer, visit him now. Go — send him off on his way into the darkness. Stand in his doorway, that's all.... You ought to do it, you ought to!” Alyosha finished, leaning hard on the word ‘ought.’
“I ought to... but I can't....” Katya moaned. “He'll look at me.... I can't.”
“Your eyes ought to meet. How will you go on living your whole life, if you don't make up your mind to do this now?”
“Better to suffer my whole life.”
“You ought to go, you ought to go,” Alyosha repeated, with merciless insistence.
“But why today, why right now?... I can't leave our patient—”
“You can spare a moment. It will only take a moment. If you don't come, he'll be delirious by tonight. I wouldn't lie to you — have pity on him!”
“Have pity on me!” Katya said, with bitter reproach, and burst into tears.
“Then you'll come,” Alyosha said firmly, seeing her tears. “I'll go and tell him you're coming right away.”
“No — don't you dare tell him that,” Katya cried in alarm. “I'll come, but don't tell him beforehand, because I might go there and not go in.... I don't know yet—”
Her voice gave out. She gasped for breath. Alyosha got up to leave.
“And what if I run into someone?” she said suddenly, in a low voice, going white again.
“That's exactly why you should go now — to avoid running into anyone. There'll be no one there, I can promise you that. We'll be expecting you,” he finished firmly, and left the room.

title: II. For A Moment The Lie Becomes Truth
paragraphs: He hurried off to the hospital where Mitya now lay. The day after his fate was decided, Mitya had come down with nervous fever and been sent to the prison ward of the town hospital. But at the request of several people (Alyosha, Madame Hohlakov, Lise, and others), Doctor Varvinsky had placed Mitya not among the other prisoners, but in a small separate room — the same one where Smerdyakov had once stayed. True, there was a sentry posted at the far end of the corridor, and a grating over the window, so Varvinsky could feel reasonably at ease about the leniency he'd shown, even though it wasn't strictly legal; but he was a kindhearted, compassionate young man. He understood how hard it would be for a man like Mitya to be thrown straight into the company of robbers and murderers, and that he needed time to adjust gradually. Visits from relatives and friends were informally allowed by the doctor and the overseer, even by the police captain. But only Alyosha and Grushenka had actually come to see Mitya. Rakitin had tried twice to force his way in, but Mitya kept begging Varvinsky not to let him.

Alyosha found him sitting on his bed in a hospital dressing gown, somewhat feverish, a towel soaked in vinegar and water wrapped around his head. He looked at Alyosha as he came in with an unreadable expression, though something like dread was visible in it. He'd grown terribly preoccupied since the trial; sometimes he'd fall silent for half an hour at a stretch, seeming to brood heavily and painfully over something, oblivious to everything around him. When he roused himself and started talking, he always spoke abruptly, and never about what was really on his mind. Sometimes he looked at his brother with a face full of suffering. He seemed more at ease with Grushenka than with Alyosha. True, he barely spoke to her at all, but the moment she walked in, his whole face lit up with joy.

Alyosha sat down beside him on the bed without a word. This time Mitya was waiting for him in suspense, but didn't dare come out and ask. He felt it was almost unthinkable that Katya would agree to come, and at the same time felt that if she didn't, something unimaginable would happen. Alyosha understood exactly what he was feeling.

“Trifon Borissovitch,” Mitya began nervously, “has torn his whole inn apart, I hear. Pulled up the flooring, ripped apart the planks, taken the whole gallery to pieces — so they tell me. He's hunting for treasure the whole time — that fifteen hundred roubles the prosecutor said I'd hidden there. Started playing these games the moment he got home, apparently. Serves him right, the swindler! The guard here told me yesterday — he's from those parts.”
“Listen,” Alyosha began. “She'll come — but I don't know when. Maybe today, maybe in a few days, I can't say. But she'll come — she will, that's certain.”

Mitya started; he seemed about to say something, but stayed silent. The news had a tremendous effect on him. It was obvious he was desperate to know exactly what had been said, but he was afraid to ask again. Anything cruel or contemptuous from Katya would have cut him like a knife at that moment.
“Among other things, she said this — that I should make sure to set your conscience at rest about the escape. If Ivan isn't well by then, she'll see to everything herself.”
“You've told me that already,” Mitya said thoughtfully.
“And you've told Grusha, too,” Alyosha observed.

“Yes,” Mitya admitted. “She won't come this morning.” He looked timidly at his brother. “She won't come until evening. When I told her yesterday that Katya was taking steps, she went quiet — but her mouth set. She only whispered, ‘Let her!’ She understood it mattered. I didn't dare push her any further. I think she understands now that Katya doesn't care for me anymore — that she loves Ivan.”
“Does she?” broke from Alyosha.

“Maybe she doesn't. But she's not coming this morning, that's for sure,” Mitya hurried to explain again. “I asked her to do something for me. You know, Ivan is better than all the rest of us. He ought to live — not us. He'll get well.”
“Would you believe it — though Katya's frightened for him, she hardly doubts he'll recover,” said Alyosha.
“That means she's convinced he'll die. It's exactly because she's so frightened that she's certain he'll get well.”
“Ivan has a strong constitution, and I believe too that there's every hope he'll recover,” Alyosha said, with some anxiety.
“Yes, he'll get well. But she's convinced he'll die. She's got a great deal of grief ahead of her....” A silence followed. Some heavy worry was gnawing at Mitya.
“Alyosha, I love Grusha terribly,” he said suddenly, in a shaking, tearful voice.
“They won't let her come out there with you,” Alyosha put in at once.

“And there's something else I wanted to tell you,” Mitya went on, a new edge suddenly in his voice. “If they beat me on the way there, or once I'm there, I won't stand for it. I'll kill someone, and I'll be shot for it. And this is supposed to go on for twenty years! They already talk to me rudely as it is. I've been lying here all night, sitting in judgment on myself. I'm not ready! I can't resign myself to it. I wanted to sing a ‘hymn’ — but if a guard so much as speaks rudely to me, I don't have the strength to bear it. For Grusha's sake I could bear anything... anything except being beaten.... But they won't even let her come there.”
Alyosha smiled gently.

“Listen, brother, once and for all,” he said. “This is what I think about it. And you know I wouldn't lie to you. Listen: you're not ready, and that kind of cross isn't meant for you. What's more, you don't need a martyr's cross like that when you're not ready for it. If you had murdered our father, it would grieve me to see you refuse your punishment. But you're innocent, and that cross is too heavy for you. You wanted to make yourself into a new man through suffering — I say, just remember that other man, always, your whole life, wherever you go, and that will be enough for you. Refusing that great cross will only leave you with an even deeper sense of duty for the rest of your life, and that constant feeling will do more, perhaps, to remake you than actually going through with it. Because out there, you wouldn't be able to bear it — you'd resent it, and in the end you might well say, ‘I owe them nothing now.’ The lawyer was right about that. Burdens as heavy as that aren't for everyone. For some men they're simply impossible. That's what I think, if you really want to know. If other men would have to answer for your escape — officers, soldiers — then I wouldn't ‘allow’ it,” Alyosha smiled. “But they say — the superintendent at that stopping point told Ivan himself — that if it's handled properly there won't be much of an inquiry, and they can get away with it easily. Of course, bribery is dishonest even in a case like this, but I can't undertake to judge that, because if Ivan and Katya asked me to act for you, I know I'd go and pay the bribes myself. I have to tell you the truth. And so I can't sit in judgment on your own decision. But let me assure you — I will never condemn you for it. And it would be strange indeed if I could judge you on this. Now I think I've covered everything.”

“But I condemn myself!” Mitya cried. “I'll escape — that much was decided without you; could Mitya Karamazov do anything else but run? But I'll condemn myself for it, and I'll pray for my sin forever. That's how the Jesuits talk, isn't it? Just like we're doing now?”
“Yes.” Alyosha smiled gently.

“I love you because you always tell the whole truth and never hide a thing,” Mitya cried, with a joyful laugh. “So I've caught my own Alyosha being a Jesuit. I have to kiss you for that. Now listen to the rest — I'll open up the other side of my heart to you. Here's what I've planned, what I've decided. If I escape — even with money and papers, even to America — I'll be cheered by the thought that I'm not running off for pleasure, not for happiness, but into another kind of exile, maybe just as bad as Siberia. It is just as bad, Alyosha, it is! I already hate that America, damn it. Even with Grusha at my side. Just look at her — is she some American? She's Russian, Russian to the marrow of her bones — she'll be homesick for the motherland, and I'll see it every single hour, that she's suffering for my sake, that she's taken up that cross for me. And what has she ever done wrong? And how am I supposed to put up with the rabble out there, even if every one of them turns out to be better than I am? I already hate that America! And even if they're wonders at machinery, the lot of them, damn them, they're not kindred souls of mine. I love Russia, Alyosha, I love the Russian God, even though I'm a scoundrel myself. I'll choke out there!” he exclaimed, his eyes suddenly blazing. His voice shook with tears. “So here's what I've decided, Alyosha, listen,” he began again, getting his emotion under control. “The moment we arrive there with Grusha, we'll go straight to work on the land, somewhere remote, in solitude, among the wild bears. There must be some remote corner even out there. I'm told there are still Redskins somewhere, way out on the edge of the horizon. So — off to the land of the Last of the Mohicans, and there Grusha and I will tackle the grammar right away. Work and grammar — that's how we'll spend three years. And by the end of it we'll speak English like a couple of Englishmen. And the moment we've learned it — goodbye, America! We'll come running back here to Russia, as American citizens. Don't worry — we won't come to this little town. We'll hide somewhere far off, north or south. I'll be a different man by then, and so will she, over there in America. The doctors will fix me up with some kind of wart on my face — what's the use of them being so mechanical otherwise! — or else I'll put out one eye, grow my beard a yard long, and turn gray pining for Russia. I dare say they won't even recognize us. And if they do, let them send us to Siberia — I don't care. It'll only mean that was our fate. We'll work the land here too, somewhere out in the wilds, and I'll play the American my whole life long. But we'll die on our own soil. That's my plan, and it's final. Do you approve?”
“Yes,” said Alyosha, not wanting to argue with him. Mitya paused for a moment, then said suddenly:
“And how they built it all up at the trial! Didn't they just build it up!”
“If they hadn't, you'd have been convicted just the same,” Alyosha said, with a sigh.
“Yes — people here are sick of the sight of me! God bless them, but it's hard,” Mitya moaned miserably. Again there was a moment of silence.
“Alyosha, put me out of my misery right now!” he burst out suddenly. “Tell me — is she coming now, or isn't she? Tell me! What did she say? How did she say it?”
“She said she'd come, but I don't know if it'll be today. It's hard for her, you know,” Alyosha said, glancing timidly at his brother.

“I should think it's hard for her! Alyosha, it'll drive me out of my mind. Grusha keeps watching me. She understands. My God, calm my heart down — what is it I even want? I want Katya! Do I even understand what I want? It's this headstrong, wicked Karamazov spirit! No — I'm not fit for suffering. I'm a scoundrel, that's all there is to say.”
“Here she is!” Alyosha cried.

At that instant Katya appeared in the doorway. For a moment she stood frozen, staring at Mitya with a dazed expression. He sprang impulsively to his feet, and a frightened look crossed his face. He went pale, but a timid, pleading smile appeared on his lips at once, and with an irresistible impulse he stretched out both hands to Katya. Seeing this, she rushed toward him. She seized his hands and, almost by force, made him sit down on the bed. She sat beside him, still gripping his hands, pressing them hard. Several times they both tried to speak, but stopped short and simply stared at each other in silence, a strange smile on both their faces, their eyes locked. Two minutes passed like this.
“Have you forgiven me?” Mitya finally faltered, and at the same instant, turning to Alyosha, his face working with joy, cried, “Do you hear what I'm asking, do you hear?”

“That's exactly what I loved you for — that generous heart of yours!” burst from Katya. “My forgiveness is no use to you, and yours is no use to me. Whether you forgive me or not, you'll always be a sore spot in my heart, and I in yours — that's simply how it has to be....” She stopped to catch her breath. “What did I come here for?” she began again, with nervous haste. “To embrace your feet, to press your hands like this, until it hurts — remember how I used to squeeze them in Moscow? — to tell you again that you're my god, my joy, to tell you that I love you madly,” she moaned in anguish, and suddenly pressed his hand greedily to her lips. Tears streamed from her eyes. Alyosha stood speechless, dumbfounded — he had never expected what he was seeing now.

“Love is over, Mitya!” Katya began again. “But the past is painfully dear to me. Know that it will always be that way. But now — for just one minute — let what might have been come true,” she faltered, a strained smile on her face, gazing at him again with a kind of joy. “You love another woman, and I love another man, and yet I will love you forever, and you'll love me — do you know that? Do you hear me? Love me — love me your whole life!” she cried, a quiver almost like a threat in her voice.

“I will love you, and... do you know, Katya,” Mitya began, drawing a deep breath between each word, “do you know, five days ago — that very evening — I loved you.... When you fell and they carried you out... All my life! So it will be, so it will always be—”
So they murmured frantic words to one another, almost meaningless, maybe not even true, but at that moment it was all true, and they both believed every word of it without question.
“Katya,” Mitya cried suddenly, “do you believe I murdered him? I know you don't believe it now — but back then... when you gave your testimony.... Surely, surely you didn't believe it!”

“I didn't believe it even then. I've never believed it. I hated you, and for a moment I talked myself into it. While I was giving my testimony I convinced myself, and believed it — but the moment I finished speaking I stopped believing it at once. Don't doubt that! I'd forgotten I came here to punish myself,” she said, a new note in her voice now, utterly unlike the loving tone of a moment before.
“Woman, yours is a heavy burden to bear,” broke, almost involuntarily, from Mitya.
“Let me go,” she whispered. “I'll come again. It's more than I can bear right now.”

She was rising to leave, but suddenly let out a loud scream and staggered back. Grushenka had come into the room, suddenly and without a sound. No one had expected her. Katya moved swiftly toward the door, but when she reached Grushenka she stopped short, turned white as chalk, and murmured, almost in a whisper:
“Forgive me!”
Grushenka stared at her, and after a moment's pause, answered in a vindictive, venomous voice:
“We're both full of hatred, my girl — you and I! Both of us, full of hatred! As if we could ever forgive each other! Save him, and I'll worship you for the rest of my life.”
“You won't forgive her!” Mitya cried, in frantic reproach.
“Don't worry — I'll save him for you!” Katya whispered rapidly, and ran out of the room.
“And you could refuse to forgive her, when she herself begged your forgiveness?” Mitya exclaimed bitterly again.
“Mitya, don't you dare blame her — you have no right to!” Alyosha cried hotly.
“Her proud lips were talking, not her heart,” Grushenka said, in a tone of disgust. “If she saves you, I'll forgive her everything—”
She fell silent, as though holding something back. She still hadn't recovered herself. She'd come in, as it turned out afterward, purely by chance, with no idea what she'd find.
“Alyosha, run after her!” Mitya cried to his brother. “Tell her... I don't know... don't let her leave like this!”
“I'll come back to see you tonight,” Alyosha said, and ran after Katya. He caught up with her outside the hospital grounds. She was walking fast, but the moment Alyosha reached her, she said quickly:

“No — in front of that woman, I can't punish myself! I asked for her forgiveness because I wanted to punish myself to the very end. She wouldn't forgive me.... I like her for that!” she added, in a strained voice, her eyes flashing with fierce resentment.
“My brother didn't expect this in the least,” Alyosha muttered. “He was sure she wouldn't come—”

“No doubt. Let's leave that alone,” she snapped. “Listen: I can't go with you to the funeral now. I've already sent them flowers. I believe they still have some money. If it's needed, tell them I'll never abandon them.... Now leave me — please, leave me. You're already late as it is — the bells are ringing for the service.... Leave me, please!”

title: III. Ilusha’s Funeral. The Speech At The Stone
paragraphs: He really was late. They had waited for him, and had already decided to carry the pretty little flower-decked coffin to the church without him. It was the coffin of poor little Ilusha. He had died two days after Mitya was sentenced. At the gate of the house, Alyosha was met by the shouts of the boys, Ilusha's schoolmates. They'd all been waiting for him impatiently and were glad he'd finally come. There were about twelve of them, all with their satchels or school-bags slung over their shoulders. “Father will cry — stay with father,” Ilusha had told them as he lay dying, and the boys had remembered. Kolya Krassotkin was in front of them all.

“I'm so glad you've come, Karamazov!” he cried, holding out his hand to Alyosha. “It's awful here. Really horrible to see. Snegiryov isn't drunk — we know for a fact he hasn't touched a drop today — but he looks as though he were.... I'm always the manly type, but this is awful. Karamazov, if I'm not holding you up, one question before we go in?”
“What is it, Kolya?” said Alyosha.
“Is your brother innocent, or guilty? Was it him who killed your father, or the valet? Whatever you say, that's how it'll be for me. I haven't slept the last four nights, thinking about it.”
“The valet killed him. My brother is innocent,” Alyosha answered.
“That's exactly what I said!” cried Smurov.
“So he'll die an innocent victim!” Kolya exclaimed. “Though he's ruined, he's happy! I could almost envy him!”
“What do you mean? How can you say that? Why?” Alyosha cried, surprised.
“Oh, if only I, too, could sacrifice myself someday for the truth!” said Kolya, with enthusiasm.
“But not in a cause like that — not with such disgrace, such horror!” said Alyosha.
“Of course.... I'd like to die for all humanity, and as for disgrace, that doesn't matter to me — our names can perish. I respect your brother!”
“So do I!” the boy who had once declared he knew who founded Troy cried out, suddenly and unexpectedly, blushing to the tips of his ears, red as a peony, just as he had that other time.

Alyosha went into the room. Ilusha lay with his hands folded, his eyes closed, in a blue coffin trimmed with a white frill. His thin face had barely changed, and strangely enough, there was no smell of decay from the body. His expression was serious, almost thoughtful. His hands, folded across his chest, looked especially beautiful, as though carved from marble. There were flowers in his hands, and the coffin, inside and out, was decked with flowers, sent early that morning by Lise Hohlakov. But there were flowers from Katerina Ivanovna too, and when Alyosha opened the door, the captain had a bunch clutched in his trembling hands and was scattering them, yet again, over his beloved boy. He barely glanced at Alyosha when he came in, and wouldn't look at anyone at all — not even at his deranged, weeping wife, ‘mamma,’ who kept trying to stand on her crippled legs to get a closer look at her dead son. Nina had been wheeled in her chair right up beside the coffin by the boys. She sat with her head pressed against it, weeping quietly too, no doubt. Snegiryov's face looked eager, yet bewildered and exasperated at once. There was something unhinged about his movements, about the words that kept bursting out of him. ‘Old man, dear old man!’ he exclaimed every minute, gazing at Ilusha. It had been his habit to call Ilusha ‘old man’ as a term of affection while he was alive.

“Father, give me a flower too — take that white one out of his hand and give it to me,” the deranged mother begged, whimpering. Whether it was because the little white rose in Ilusha's hand had caught her fancy, or because she wanted one from his own hand to keep in his memory, she stirred restlessly, reaching out her hands for the flower.
“I won't give it to anyone — I won't give you anything,” Snegiryov cried, coldly. “These are his flowers, not yours! Everything here is his, nothing is yours!”
“Father, give mother a flower!” said Nina, lifting a face wet with tears.

“I won't give anything away, and to her least of all! She never loved Ilusha. She took away his little cannon, and he gave it to her,” the captain broke into loud sobs at the memory of how Ilusha had given up his cannon to his mother. The poor, deranged woman was drowned in silent tears, her face hidden in her hands.
The boys, seeing that the father wouldn't leave the coffin and that it was time to carry it out, gathered in a tight circle around it and began to lift it.
“I don't want him buried in the churchyard,” Snegiryov suddenly wailed. “I'll bury him by the stone — by our stone! Ilusha told me to. I won't let him be carried out!”
He'd been saying for the past three days that he'd bury him by the stone, but Alyosha, Krassotkin, the landlady, her sister, and all the boys argued against it.

“What an idea — to bury him by some unholy stone, as if he'd hanged himself!” the old landlady said sternly. “There in the churchyard, the ground has been blessed. He'll be prayed for there. You can hear the singing in church, and the deacon reads so clearly, so distinctly, that it'll reach him every time, just as though it were being read right over his grave.”

At last the captain made a gesture of despair, as if to say, ‘Take him wherever you like.’ The boys lifted the coffin, but as they passed the mother, they paused for a moment and lowered it so she could say goodbye to Ilusha. But at the sight of that precious little face, which for the past three days she had only seen from a distance, she trembled all over, and her gray head began twitching spasmodically over the coffin.

“Mother, make the sign of the cross over him, give him your blessing, kiss him,” Nina cried to her. But her head kept twitching like some mechanical thing, and, her face twisted with bitter grief, she began, without a word, beating her breast with her fist. They carried the coffin past her. Nina pressed her lips to her brother's for the last time as they bore it by her. As Alyosha left the house, he asked the landlady to look after those left behind, but she cut him off before he'd finished.
“Of course I'll stay with them — we're Christians too.” The old woman wept as she said it.

They didn't have far to carry the coffin to the church — no more than three hundred paces. It was a still, clear day, with a light frost. The church bells were still ringing. Snegiryov hurried along behind the coffin, fussing, distracted, in his short old summer overcoat, bareheaded, his soft old wide-brimmed hat in his hand. He seemed caught up in a kind of bewildered anxiety. One minute he'd reach out to steady the head of the coffin, only getting in the bearers' way; the next he'd run alongside, trying to find some place for himself. A flower fell onto the snow, and he lunged to pick it up as though the whole world depended on that one lost flower.

“And the crust of bread — we've forgotten the crust!” he suddenly cried out in dismay. But the boys reminded him at once that he'd already taken the crust of bread, that it was in his pocket. He pulled it out instantly and was reassured.

“Ilusha told me to, Ilusha did,” he explained at once to Alyosha. “I was sitting with him one night, and he suddenly said to me: ‘Father, when they've filled in my grave, crumble some bread over it, so the sparrows will fly down — I'll hear them, and it'll cheer me up, not lying there all alone.’”
“That's a good thing to do,” said Alyosha. “We should bring some often.”
“Every day, every day!” the captain said quickly, seeming cheered by the thought.

They reached the church at last, and set the coffin down in the middle of it. The boys gathered around it and stood there, reverent, through the whole service. It was an old, rather poor church; many of the icons had no settings — but such churches are the best for praying in. During the mass, Snegiryov grew somewhat calmer, though every so often he had another outburst of that same unconscious, almost incoherent anxiety. At one point he went up to the coffin to straighten the cover or the wreath; when a candle fell out of its holder, he rushed to put it back and fumbled over it for an agonizingly long time, then settled down again and stood quietly by the coffin, his face full of blank unease and confusion. After the Epistle, he suddenly whispered to Alyosha, standing beside him, that the Epistle hadn't been read properly — but didn't explain what he meant. During the hymn ‘Like the Cherubim,’ he joined in the singing but didn't make it to the end. Falling to his knees, he pressed his forehead to the stone floor and stayed like that for a long time.

At last came the funeral service itself, and candles were handed out. The distracted father started fussing about again, but the touching, solemn funeral prayers moved and stirred his soul. He seemed to shrink in on himself all at once and broke into quick, short sobs, which he tried at first to stifle, but at last sobbed openly. When they began saying their farewells to the dead boy and closing the coffin, he flung his arms about, as though he wouldn't let them cover Ilusha, and began kissing his dead son's lips greedily, over and over. At last they managed to talk him down from the step, but he suddenly reached out and snatched a few flowers from the coffin. He looked at them, and some new idea seemed to dawn on him, so that for a moment he seemed to forget his grief entirely. Gradually he sank into a kind of brooding, and didn't resist when the coffin was lifted and carried to the grave. It was an expensive plot, close to the church, in the churchyard — Katerina Ivanovna had paid for it. After the customary rites, the gravediggers lowered the coffin. Snegiryov, flowers still in hand, bent so far over the open grave that the boys grabbed his coat in alarm and pulled him back. He didn't seem to fully grasp what was happening. When they began filling in the grave, he suddenly pointed anxiously at the falling earth and tried to say something, but no one could make out what he meant, and he broke off suddenly. Then they reminded him he had to crumble the bread, and he grew terribly excited, snatched up the loaf, began pulling it apart, and flung the pieces onto the grave.
“Come on, fly down, birds — fly down, sparrows!” he muttered anxiously.

One of the boys pointed out that it was awkward for him to crumble the bread with the flowers still in his hands, and suggested he give them to someone to hold for a while. But he wouldn't hear of it, and in fact seemed suddenly alarmed for his flowers, as though someone might try to take them away from him entirely. And after looking over the grave, satisfying himself, it seemed, that everything had been done and the bread duly crumbled, he suddenly, to everyone's surprise, turned around quite calmly and set off for home. But his steps grew quicker and quicker, until he was almost running. The boys and Alyosha kept pace with him.
“The flowers are for mamma, the flowers are for mamma! I was unkind to mamma,” he suddenly began exclaiming.

Someone called out for him to put his hat on, since it was cold. But he flung the hat down in the snow as if in anger, repeating, ‘I won't wear the hat, I won't wear the hat.’ Smurov picked it up and carried it after him. All the boys were crying, Kolya and the boy who'd discovered Troy crying hardest of all. Though Smurov, with the captain's hat in hand, was crying bitterly too, he still managed, as he ran, to snatch up a piece of red brick lying in the snow on the path and fling it at a flock of sparrows flying past. He missed, of course, and kept on crying as he ran. Halfway there, Snegiryov suddenly stopped short, stood frozen for half a minute as though struck by something, then turned back toward the church and ran for the abandoned grave. But the boys caught up with him at once and seized him on every side. He collapsed onto the snow as though knocked down, and, struggling, sobbing, wailing, began crying out, ‘Ilusha, old man, dear old man!’ Alyosha and Kolya tried to get him up, soothing him, coaxing him.
“Captain, that's enough — a brave man has to show some fortitude,” Kolya muttered.
“You'll ruin the flowers,” said Alyosha, “and mamma's waiting for them — she's sitting there crying because you wouldn't give her any before. Ilusha's little bed is still there—”

“Yes, yes, mamma!” Snegiryov suddenly remembered. “They'll take away the bed — they'll take it away,” he added, as though genuinely afraid it would happen. He jumped up and ran home again. But it wasn't far, and they all arrived together. Snegiryov threw open the door in a hurry and called to his wife, the very woman he'd quarreled with so cruelly not long before:

“Mamma, my poor crippled darling, Ilusha has sent you these flowers,” he cried, holding out to her a small bunch of flowers, frozen and crushed from his struggle in the snow. But at that same moment he caught sight, in the corner by the little bed, of Ilusha's little boots, which the landlady had set neatly side by side. At the sight of those old, patched, rust-colored, stiffened boots, he threw up his hands and rushed toward them, dropped to his knees, snatched up one boot, and, pressing his lips to it, began kissing it greedily, crying, ‘Ilusha, old man, dear old man, where are your little feet?’”

“Where have you taken him? Where have you taken him?” the poor demented woman cried, in a heartbreaking voice. Nina, too, broke into sobs. Kolya ran out of the room, and the other boys followed him. At last Alyosha went out as well.
“Let them cry,” he said to Kolya. “There's no use trying to comfort them right now. Let's wait a minute, then go back in.”

“No, it's no use — it's awful,” Kolya agreed. “Do you know, Karamazov,” he dropped his voice so no one else could hear, “I feel terribly sad, and if there were any way to bring him back, I'd give anything in the world to do it.”
“So would I,” said Alyosha.
“What do you think, Karamazov? Should we come back here tonight? He'll be drunk, you know.”

“Maybe he will. Let's come together, you and I — that will be enough, to spend an hour with them, with the mother and Nina. If we all come at once, we'll only remind them of everything all over again,” Alyosha suggested.
“The landlady's laying the table for them now — there'll be some kind of funeral dinner, the priest is coming. Shall we go back for it, Karamazov?”
“Of course,” said Alyosha.
“It's all so strange, Karamazov — such grief, and then pancakes right after it. It seems so unnatural, somehow, in our religion.”
“They're going to have salmon, too,” the boy who'd discovered Troy remarked, loudly.

“I'll ask you most earnestly, Kartashov, not to interrupt again with your idiotic remarks — especially when no one is talking to you, and no one particularly cares whether you exist or not!” Kolya snapped irritably. The boy flushed crimson but didn't dare answer back.
Meanwhile they'd been strolling slowly along the path, and suddenly Smurov exclaimed:
“There's Ilusha's stone — the one they wanted to bury him under.”

They all stopped by the big stone. Alyosha looked at it, and the whole scene Snegiryov had described to him that day rose up at once before his mind's eye — how Ilusha, weeping, clinging to his father, had cried, ‘Father, father, how he insulted you.’
A sudden impulse seemed to rise up in his soul. With a serious, earnest expression, he looked from one bright, pleasant face to another among Ilusha's schoolmates, and suddenly said to them:
“Boys, I'd like to say one thing to you, here, at this spot.”
The boys gathered around him and at once turned attentive, expectant eyes on him.

“Boys, we'll be parting soon. For a while I'll be staying with my two brothers — one of whom is bound for Siberia, and the other lying close to death. But soon I'll be leaving this town, perhaps for a long time, so we're going to part. Let's make a promise here, at Ilusha's stone, that we'll never forget Ilusha, or one another. And whatever happens to us later in life, even if we don't meet again for twenty years, let's always remember how we buried this poor boy — the one we once threw stones at, do you remember, by the bridge? — and how we all grew so fond of him afterward. He was a fine boy — kindhearted, brave — he cared about his father's honor, resented the cruel insult done to him, and stood up for him. And so, first of all, let's remember him, boys, for the rest of our lives. And even if we get caught up in the most important things in the world, even if we rise to great honor or fall into great misfortune — let's still remember how good it was, once, here, when we were all together, bound by a good, kind feeling that made us, for as long as we loved that poor boy, better people than we are, perhaps, the rest of the time. My little doves — let me call you that, because right now, looking at your good, dear faces, you remind me so much of them, those pretty blue birds. My dear children, maybe you won't understand what I'm telling you, because I often speak rather unclearly, but you'll remember it all the same, and you'll agree with me someday. You should know that there's nothing higher, nothing stronger, nothing healthier or more useful for life afterward than some good memory — especially a memory from childhood, from home. People talk to you endlessly about your education, but some good, sacred memory, kept safe from childhood, may be the best education of all. If a man carries many such memories with him into life, he's safe to the end of his days — and even if a person has only one good memory left in his heart, that alone might someday be enough to save him. Perhaps we'll even grow wicked as we get older, unable to resist some bad action, laughing at people's tears, at those who say, as Kolya just said, ‘I want to suffer for all mankind’ — we might even sneer spitefully at people like that. But however wicked we may become — God forbid — still, when we remember how we buried Ilusha, how we loved him in his last days, and how we've been talking together like friends, right here, at this stone — even the cruelest, most mocking among us, if that's what we become, won't dare, inside himself, to laugh at having been kind and good in this moment! What's more — perhaps that one memory alone will keep him from some great evil, and he'll stop and say to himself, ‘Yes, I was good and brave and honest once.’ Let him laugh to himself if he wants — that's no matter; people often laugh at what's good and kind. That's only thoughtlessness. But I promise you, boys, that even as he laughs, he'll say at once, in his heart, ‘No — I'm wrong to laugh, because that's nothing to laugh at.’”
“That will be so — I understand you, Karamazov!” Kolya cried, his eyes shining.
The boys were stirred, and they wanted to say something too, but held themselves back, watching the speaker with rapt, emotional attention.

“I'm saying this in case we turn out bad,” Alyosha went on, “but there's no reason we should turn out bad, is there, boys? Let's be, first and above all, kind — then honest — and then let's never forget each other! I say it again. I give you my word, for my part, that I'll never forget a single one of you. Every face looking at me right now, I'll remember, even thirty years from now. Just a moment ago, Kolya told Kartashov that we didn't care whether he existed or not. But I can't forget that Kartashov exists, and that he isn't blushing now, the way he did when he discovered who founded Troy, but is looking at me with his cheerful, kind, dear little eyes. Boys, my dear boys, let's all be generous and brave, like Ilusha, clever and brave and generous like Kolya (though he'll be far cleverer still once he's grown), and let's all be as modest, as clever, as sweet as Kartashov. But why am I singling out just those two? All of you are dear to me, boys, from this day on — I've kept a place in my heart for every one of you, and I ask you to keep a place in your hearts for me too! Well then — who was it who brought us together in this good, kind feeling, which we'll remember, and mean to remember, our whole lives long? Who, if not Ilusha — the good boy, the dear boy, precious to us forever! Let's never forget him. May his memory live forever in our hearts, from this moment on!”
“Yes, yes, forever, forever!” the boys cried out, in ringing voices, their faces softened.
“Let's remember his face, and his clothes, and his poor little boots, his coffin, and his unhappy, sinful father, and how bravely he stood up for him, alone, against the whole school.”
“We will remember, we will remember,” the boys cried. “He was brave, he was good!”
“Ah, how I loved him!” Kolya exclaimed.
“Ah, children, ah, dear friends — don't be afraid of life! How good life is, when you do something good and just!”
“Yes, yes,” the boys repeated, enthusiastically.
“Karamazov, we love you!” a voice — Kartashov's, probably — cried out impulsively.
“We love you, we love you!” they all took it up. Tears stood in many of their eyes.
“Hurrah for Karamazov!” Kolya shouted, in an ecstasy.
“And may the dead boy's memory live forever!” Alyosha added again, with feeling.
“Forever!” the boys chimed in again.
“Karamazov,” Kolya cried, “can it really be true, what religion teaches us — that we'll all rise again from the dead, and live, and see each other again — everyone, Ilusha too?”
“Certainly we'll all rise again, certainly we'll see each other again, and tell each other, with joy and gladness, everything that's happened!” Alyosha answered, half laughing, half in earnest.
“Ah, how wonderful that will be!” burst from Kolya.

“Well, now let's finish talking and go to his funeral dinner. Don't mind us eating pancakes — it's a very old custom, and there's something good in that!” Alyosha laughed. “Come, let's go! And now, we go hand in hand.”
“And always like this, hand in hand, our whole lives long! Hurrah for Karamazov!” Kolya cried once more, rapturously, and once again the boys took up his cry: ‘Hurrah for Karamazov!’
